prompt: Is there a general method for solving a first-price sealed-bid auction with two bidders who have independent private values drawn from different distributions (i.e., ex-ante asymmetric bidders)?
article:
# Solving two‑bidder first‑price sealed‑bid auctions with independent private values and ex‑ante asymmetry

## Executive summary
Two‑bidder first‑price sealed‑bid auctions (FPSBAs) with independent private values (IPV) and differing value distributions (ex‑ante asymmetry) are a canonical but technically challenging class of auction games. Closed‑form solutions exist only in simple/symmetric cases (e.g., i.i.d. Uniform), while the general asymmetric case requires solving a coupled system of first‑order conditions that typically reduce to integral equations or ordinary differential equations (ODEs). Practical solution methods include (a) analytical characterizations for special cases, (b) perturbation/asymptotic expansions for small asymmetries, (c) numerical solution techniques (discretization, collocation, best‑response iteration, Newton methods), and (d) empirical/inversion methods to recover value distributions from bid data. Asymmetry changes equilibrium bid shading, winning probabilities, and seller revenue; strong (stochastically larger) bidders shade differently and generally obtain higher payoffs. Risk aversion, budget constraints or non‑overlapping supports introduce further qualitative changes (bifurcations, discontinuities). Core references and applied recipes for solving and estimating these models are given below.

## Model setup and notation

- Two bidders i = 1, 2. Bidder i’s private value Vi is drawn independently from Fi with density fi on support [ai, bi]. Distributions Fi need not be identical (ex‑ante asymmetry).
- Bids are submitted simultaneously and sealed. Highest bid wins and pays her bid (first‑price). Ties broken by rule (irrelevant for continuous distributions).
- Strategy: bidder i uses a strictly increasing, measurable bidding function βi : [ai, bi] → R+, so a realized value v maps to bid b = βi(v). Inverse φi = βi^{-1} exists on the relevant bid range.
- Payoff for bidder i with value v who bids b is (v − b) · Pr(win with b) = (v − b) · Pj(b), where Pj(b) = Pr(βj(Vj) ≤ b) = Fj(φj(b)).
- Equilibrium concept: Bayes‑Nash equilibrium (BNE) in pure strategies (monotone increasing βi). See standard IPV/Bayesian game formulation [THE THEORY OF FIRST‑PRICE, SEALED‑BID AUCTIONS](https://eml.berkeley.edu/~mcfadden/eC103_f03/auctionlect.pdf) [1], [First‑Price Sealed‑Bid Auctions | Brown CS](https://cs.brown.edu/courses/cs1951k/lectures/2020/first_price_auctions.pdf) [2].

## Symmetric benchmark (closed‑form and intuition)
- When bidders are symmetric (Fi = F for both) and risk‑neutral, a unique increasing symmetric BNE b(v) exists and is given by the standard formula (for n bidders):
  b(v) = v − ∫_0^v [F(x)]^{n−1} dx / [F(v)]^{n−1}.
  For n = 2 this simplifies to
  b(v) = v − ∫_0^v F(x) dx / F(v).
  For example, with Vi ∼ U(0,1), b(v) = (n−1)/n · v → for n = 2, b(v) = v/2 [2],[3].
- Symmetric closed‑form solutions provide intuition: bid shading equals expected rival maximum conditional on losing; more bidders → less shading.

References: [THE THEORY OF FIRST‑PRICE, SEALED‑BID AUCTIONS](https://eml.berkeley.edu/~mcfadden/eC103_f03/auctionlect.pdf) [1], [First‑Price Sealed‑Bid Auctions | Brown CS](https://cs.brown.edu/courses/cs1951k/lectures/2020/first_price_auctions.pdf) [2], [Auction Theory (Krishna notes)](https://bugarinmauricio.com/wp-content/uploads/2017/06/krishna-auction-theory-caps1a4.pdf) [3].

## What changes under ex‑ante asymmetry?
- Asymmetry = Fi ≠ Fj. Key implications:
  - Equilibrium strategies are generally asymmetric: β1 ≠ β2 and cannot be obtained by a simple scalar multiple of valuations.
  - Equilibrium characterization reduces to a coupled system of (nonlinear) differential/integral equations; closed forms are rare except for special distributional pairs.
  - Stronger bidders (those whose Fi stochastically dominates the other) tend to win more often but also shade bids differently; they may shade more or less depending on details (often more shading if they’re more likely to have a high value) [Asymmetric Auctions (Maskin)](https://scholar.harvard.edu/files/maskin/files/asymmetric_auctions.pdf) [4].
  - Revenue consequences can be counterintuitive: small asymmetries often raise seller revenue relative to symmetric baseline in some settings (especially with heterogenous risk aversion) but can reduce it in others; first‑price vs second‑price revenue ranking may flip under resale or asymmetric information [5],[8],[9].

Key discussions: [Asymmetric Auctions (Maskin)](https://scholar.harvard.edu/files/maskin/files/asymmetric_auctions.pdf) [4], [First‑price sealed‑bid auctions when bidders exhibit different ...](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/abs/pii/S0165176511002473) [8].

## Theoretical characterization for two asymmetric bidders

### First‑order condition (economic intuition)
- For bidder i with valuation v, the expected payoff from bidding b is (v − b) · Fj(φj(b)). At an interior optimum b = βi(v), the first‑order condition (FOC) sets the derivative w.r.t b equal to zero. Evaluated at equilibrium, this FOC ties βi and βj together through fj and Fj (via φj and βj′). This produces a coupled system that, after algebra, can be written as a pair of integral/ODE conditions linking β1 and β2 (see Maskin and later analytic expositions) [4],[7].

### Differential/integral equation form (qualitative statement)
- The equilibrium pair {β1, β2} satisfies a pair of functional equations that are equivalent to a system of first‑order ODEs (or integral equations). The general solution method is to:
  - Express the FOC for each bidder i in terms of βi and the inverse φj;
  - Differentiate appropriately to obtain ODEs for βi (or φi) with boundary conditions at the lower support endpoints (usually βi(ai) = ai or zero depending on normalization);
  - Solve the coupled system subject to monotonicity and boundary conditions.
- Closed forms are exceptional; existence and uniqueness results exist under regularity conditions (continuous densities, monotonicity) but solutions require numerical or perturbation methods in general [4],[5],[7].

See formal expositions and proofs: [Asymmetric Auctions (Maskin)](https://scholar.harvard.edu/files/maskin/files/asymmetric_auctions.pdf) [4], and the survey/perturbation analysis [ASYMMETRIC FIRST‑PRICE AUCTIONS—A PERTURBATION ...](http://www.math.tau.ac.il/~fibich/Manuscripts/first_rev_final.pdf) [5].

## Analytical approximation: perturbation and asymptotic methods
- Small asymmetry expansion: when distributions differ only slightly (Fi = F + εGi), equilibrium strategies and revenue can be expanded in powers of ε. First‑order corrections often vanish (revenue change typically O(ε²)), so second‑order terms matter. Perturbation methods yield closed‑form approximations for bid functions and revenues useful for comparative statics [5].
- Advantages: provides insight into how small distributional differences affect bids and revenue without full numerical solutions.
- References: Fibich et al. perturbation analysis and related surveys [5].

## Numerical and computational techniques (practical recipes)

Numerical methods are the workhorse for solving general asymmetric two‑bidder FPSBAs. Common approaches:

1. Discretization + best‑response iteration
   - Discretize each support [ai, bi] on a grid {v^k}.
   - Initialize candidate strategies βi^0 (e.g., symmetric equilibrium, linear shading).
   - For each grid point v^k compute best response bid b that maximizes (v^k − b) · Fj(φj^{(t)}(b)) using root‑finding (or direct maximization).
   - Update βi^{(t+1)} and enforce monotonicity (monotone interpolation).
   - Iterate until convergence.
   - Pros: conceptually simple, reliable for moderate grids. Cons: requires care to maintain monotonicity and to invert discrete bidding functions (φj).
   - Reference algorithmic descriptions: [Numerical Analysis of Asymmetric First Price Auctions (Penn State)](https://capcp.la.psu.edu/wp-content/uploads/sites/11/numericalanalysis.pdf) [6], [Numerical Solutions of Asymmetric, First‑Price, Independent Private ...](https://capcp.la.psu.edu/wp-content/uploads/sites/11/2020/07/NumericalSolutions.pdf) [15].

2. Solve coupled ODEs / collocation
   - Reformulate equilibrium conditions as a coupled system of ODEs in βi (or inverses φi).
   - Use collocation or boundary value ODE solvers to find βi satisfying boundary conditions at the supports.
   - Practical for smooth distributions and when transforms/integrals are tractable numerically.
   - See detailed numerical collocation and Taylor expansion methods in Penn State notes [6] and Brock’s simpler approach [7].

3. Direct root‑finding on functional equations
   - Represent βi with a finite basis (polynomials, splines). Impose the equilibrium condition at collocation points and solve the resulting nonlinear system by Newton‑type methods.
   - Requires good initial guess and robust nonlinear solvers; sensitive but high precision possible.

4. Perturbation + numerical refinement
   - Use perturbation expansion to get analytic approximation as initial guess, then refine numerically (accelerates convergence and reduces computational burden) [5].

5. Computational complexity caveat
   - Computing equilibria in continuous FPSBAs is theoretically hard in general (PPAD‑complete for continuous types); practical algorithms succeed for many economically relevant cases but be mindful of local multiple equilibria and numerical stiffness [AGTA Lecture 18 — Bayesian Games and First‑Price Auctions](https://opencourse.inf.ed.ac.uk/sites/default/files/2025-03/agta_-_lecture_18_-_bayesian_games_and_first-price_auctions.pdf) [11].

Practical implementation tips:
- Use a fine grid in regions where Fi and fj change rapidly; adaptivity helps.
- Enforce monotonicity using isotonic regression or monotone splines.
- Check solutions by simulating equilibrium play: (i) sample values, (ii) compute bids, (iii) check best‑response deviations.
- Validate by checking boundary behaviour (e.g., bids near lower support) and comparative statics (e.g., limiting symmetric case recovers known b(v) = v/2 for uniform).

Detailed implementation and numerical examples are given in [Numerical Analysis of Asymmetric First Price Auctions (Penn State)](https://capcp.la.psu.edu/wp-content/uploads/sites/11/numericalanalysis.pdf) [6] and [A Simple Approach to Analyzing Asymmetric First Price Auctions](https://brocku.ca/repec/pdf/0504.pdf) [7].

## Empirical and identification methods

- Structural estimation / inversion: observed bids can be inverted to recover value distributions if equilibrium bidding functions are monotone. The classic strategy (Guerre–Perrigne–Vuong class) uses the first‑order condition to express the private value as a function of bid, estimates the bid density and distribution nonparametrically, and recovers Fi. Recent functional estimation papers adapt these methods to asymmetric settings and propose estimators/sieve methods for the inverse problem [A functional estimation approach to the first‑price auction models](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S0304407623000192) [10].
- Identification: special attention is required in asymmetric environments because each bidder’s distribution is different and the mapping from bids to values depends on the opponent’s strategy; identification relies on support overlap and monotonicity conditions [Identification of Standard Auction Models (Athey)](https://gsb-faculty.stanford.edu/susan-athey/files/2022/04/ident_0901_0.pdf) [9].
- Practical estimation requires sufficient variation and sample size; discretization/trimming and boundary corrections are important.

Further reading: [A functional estimation approach to the first‑price auction models](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S0304407623000192) [10], [Identification of Standard Auction Models (Athey)](https://gsb-faculty.stanford.edu/susan-athey/files/2022/04/ident_0901_0.pdf) [9].

## Effects of distributional shape and other extensions

- Strong vs weak bidders:
  - If F1 first‑order stochastically dominates F2 (F1 yields stochastically higher values), bidder 1 is the “strong” bidder. Strong bidders tend to win more often and capture higher expected surplus. Their bid distributions often first‑order stochastically dominate the weak bidder’s bid distribution under regularity [Asymmetric Auctions (Maskin)](https://scholar.harvard.edu/files/maskin/files/asymmetric_auctions.pdf) [4].
- Non‑overlapping supports:
  - If supports differ or do not overlap, the equilibrium can show “bid bifurcation” — bids can separate into distinct regions (weak bidder may be effectively excluded). See multi‑bidder generalizations and bifurcation analysis [Asymmetric Auctions with More Than Two Bidders](https://www.uoguelph.ca/economics/repec/workingpapers/2015/2015-02.pdf) [12].
- Risk aversion and budgets:
  - Risk aversion increases shading in first‑price auctions and can amplify the effects of asymmetry: seller revenue often increases with asymmetry in risk aversion and can change ranking between auction formats [First‑price sealed‑bid auctions when bidders exhibit different ...](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/abs/pii/S0165176511002473) [8], [Asymmetric Auctions (Maskin)](https://scholar.harvard.edu/files/maskin/files/asymmetric_auctions.pdf) [4].
  - Private budget constraints can produce discontinuities and multiple equilibria [Penn State numerical notes; theory papers].
- Resale and interdependence:
  - If resale after the auction is allowed, revenue comparisons and equilibrium properties can change; in some asymmetric settings FPSBAs may yield higher revenue than second‑price auctions when resale is present [Asymmetric Auctions with Resale](https://www.mdc.e.u-tokyo.ac.jp/wp/wp-content/uploads/2025/05/Asymmetric-Auctions-with-Resale.pdf) (see broader literature).

Representative references: [5],[12],[8],[4].

## Practical applications and examples
- Procurement and reverse auctions: widely used in awarding contracts; asymmetry is natural (firms have different cost distributions). Numerical solution methods are used to model bidding and design mechanisms [First‑Price Sealed‑Bid Auctions | Brown CS](https://cs.brown.edu/courses/cs1951k/lectures/2020/first_price_auctions.pdf) [2].
- Online advertising ad exchanges: industry move from second‑price toward first‑price (header bidding) has revived applied interest in bid shading algorithms; practitioners implement real‑time bid shading using structural or heuristic approaches calibrated to opponent distributions [First‑Price Auctions for Online Advertisements - Cornell](https://blogs.cornell.edu/info2040/2019/10/24/first-price-auctions-for-online-advertisements/) [14].
- Experimental findings: laboratory studies find that human bidders often bid differently from theoretical predictions (risk aversion and other behavioral factors matter); asymmetric treatment effects observed in experiments [Bidding behavior in asymmetric auctions: An experimental study](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/abs/pii/S0014292104000753) [13].

## Step‑by‑step numerical recipe for practitioners (two bidders, risk‑neutral)
1. Specify Fi and fi on supports [ai, bi] and [aj, bj]; ensure densities > 0 on supports.
2. Create value grids Gi = {v_i^k} for both bidders; choose finer grids where fi varies rapidly.
3. Initialize βi^0 (e.g., linear shading βi^0(v) = α·v for α in (0,1) or symmetric equilibrium for an averaged F).
4. For iteration t and each grid point v_i^k:
   - Solve best response problem b* = argmax_b (v_i^k − b) · Fj(φj^{(t)}(b)), where φj^{(t)} is discrete inverse of βj^{(t)} (use interpolation).
   - Use robust 1D optimization / root finding (ensure monotone bracket).
5. Enforce monotonicity on updated βi^{(t+1)} (isotonic regression or monotone spline fit).
6. Check convergence norm ||βi^{(t+1)} − βi^{(t)}||; if not converged, repeat.
7. Validate solution by simulation: sample (V1,V2), compute bids, compute incentives to deviate numerically.
8. Optionally refine by collocation/Newton on the discretized equilibrium equations for higher accuracy.

Detailed practical algorithms and convergence diagnostics are given in [Numerical Analysis of Asymmetric First Price Auctions (Penn State)](https://capcp.la.psu.edu/wp-content/uploads/sites/11/numericalanalysis.pdf) [6] and [A Simple Approach to Analyzing Asymmetric First Price Auctions](https://brocku.ca/repec/pdf/0504.pdf) [7].

## Recommended method selection
- Analytical closed form: use only for symmetric or specially crafted distributions (Uniform, exponential with specific transformations).
- Perturbation analysis: when distributions are close (small deviations) and comparative statics are of interest [5].
- Numerical discretization/collocation: recommended in most applied cases with arbitrary Fi; combine with monotonicity enforcement and simulation checks [6],[7].
- Structural estimation / inversion: use when working with observed bid data and the goal is to recover Fi or test model predictions; requires nonparametric density estimation and support overlap [10],[9].

## Limitations, computational issues and cautions
- Multiple or non‑interior equilibria can exist in discrete or nonregular settings; numerical solvers may find local fixed points — checking best‑response incentives and global simulation is crucial.
- PPAD/complexity theory implies theoretical hardness in general continuous games; however, economic instances are usually solvable numerically with careful implementation [11].
- Empirical identification in asymmetric settings is more demanding than symmetric ones; support overlap and sufficient sample variation are essential [9],[10].
- Behavioral deviations (risk aversion, bounded rationality) can produce systematic departures from theoretical bidding strategies observed in experiments [13].

## Conclusion and practical takeaway
Analytical solutions are limited to symmetric or very special asymmetric pairs. For general two‑bidder asymmetric IPV first‑price auctions, the equilibrium is characterized by coupled functional equations typically solved using numerical methods (discretization, collocation) or approximated via perturbation when asymmetry is small. Empirical work relies on inversion/structural estimation to recover value distributions from bids. Choice of method should be driven by the degree of asymmetry, desired accuracy, computational resources, and whether the application is theoretical (comparative statics) or applied (estimation, auction design). article:
# Mitigating Material Damage to Lithium Niobate (LN) After Plasma Etching — Comprehensive Review and Practical Guidance

## Executive summary
Plasma etching of lithium niobate (LiNbO3, LN) enables high‑index‑contrast photonic structures but creates surface damage mechanisms that increase optical loss, change electro‑optical properties, and limit performance. The primary damage modes are (1) chemical by‑products redeposition (notably LiF), (2) ion‑induced amorphization and point defects, (3) micro‑masking and roughness, and (4) crystallographic‑orientation–dependent cracking/anisotropic etch features. Effective mitigation requires a toolbox of process choices (plasma chemistry, ion energy/bias, pressure, substrate temperature), materials strategies (hard masks, protective coatings, proton exchange), and post‑etch chemical and thermal treatments (acid rinses, SC‑1, oxygen anneal, re‑crystallization/ALE). The recommendations below synthesize empirical results and theoretical/chemical mechanisms from primary literature to provide actionable process guidelines and identify remaining research gaps.

## Background: damage mechanisms during LN plasma etching
- Chemical redeposition: Fluorine‑based plasmas (CF4, SF6, NF3, CHF3 mixtures) react with Li in LN to form low‑volatility LiF, which redeposits on sidewalls and surfaces, causing micro‑masking, reduced etch rate, roughness, and non‑vertical walls [Advanced Etching Techniques of LiNbO3 Nanodevices](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10609314/)[1], [Growth of crystalline LiF on CF4 plasma etched LiNbO3](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/abs/pii/S0022024898000098)[9].
- Ion bombardment damage: High‑energy ions create amorphous surface layers, oxygen vacancies and point defects that increase optical absorption and can change ferroelectric/photorefractive properties. Depth of damage scales with ion fluence and energy; heavily damaged layers may be hundreds of nm under some conditions [Advanced Etching Techniques ...](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10609314/)[1], [Lithium Niobate Reactive Ion Etching](https://apps.dtic.mil/sti/pdfs/ADA381148.pdf)[14].
- Crystallographic anisotropy: Etch rates and morphology depend strongly on crystal orientation; the −Z face typically etches fastest and y‑surfaces can show directional substructure and be more crack‑prone [Etch Rate Dependence on Crystal Orientation of Lithium Niobate](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/21041126/)[5].
- Temperature and chemistry interplay: Substrate temperature and gas mixtures alter reaction kinetics and the volatility of etch by‑products — heated substrates and oxygen‑containing mixtures often reduce redeposition and improve surface quality [The effect of a lithium niobate heating on the etching rate in SF6 ICP plasma](https://cns1.rc.fas.harvard.edu/facilities/docs/The%20effect%20of%20a%20lithium%20niobate%20heating%20on%20the%20etching%20rate%20in%20SF6%20ICP%20plasma.pdf)[6].

## Plasma etching process choices and their impact on damage
### Reactive Ion Etching (RIE) vs Inductively Coupled Plasma (ICP)
- ICP generally produces higher etch rates and better ion flux control than RIE, enabling deeper etches and steeper sidewalls; literature reports ICP etch rates of tens to >100 nm/min depending on mask and chemistry (e.g., ~79 nm/min using SF6/Ar with metal masks; reported up to ~108 nm/min with SiO2 masks and Cl‑based ICP) [Advanced Etching Techniques ...](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10609314/)[1].
- Higher ion flux and independent RF bias control in ICP allow tuning ion energy to balance physical sputtering (to avoid LiF redeposition) and minimize substrate amorphization. Processes with higher DC bias have been shown empirically to reduce redeposition [Redeposition‑free inductively‑coupled plasma etching of lithium niobate](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11501321/)[2].

### Gas chemistry: fluorine, chlorine, bromine, and mixed chemistries
- Fluorine chemistries (CF4, SF6, NF3, CHF3) efficiently etch oxides but generate LiF, a low‑volatility solid that redeposits and forms micro‑masks; this limits verticality and increases roughness [Advanced Etching Techniques ...](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10609314/)[1], [Growth of crystalline LiF ...](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/abs/pii/S0022024898000098)[9].
- Inclusion of oxygen (e.g., SF6/O2) can increase volatility of by‑products and reduce LiF deposition, improving surface quality; heated substrate + SF6/O2 produced much higher etch rates and better surface quality in empirical studies (reported maximum >800 nm/min at ~598 K under optimized conditions) [The effect of a lithium niobate heating ...](https://cns1.rc.fas.harvard.edu/facilities/docs/The%20effect%20of%20a%20lithium%20niobate%20heating%20on%20the%20etching%20rate%20in%20SF6%20ICP%20plasma.pdf)[6].
- Chlorine‑ and bromine‑based chemistries (Cl2, BCl3, HBr) have been used to reduce LiF redeposition. A directional atomic layer etching (ALE) approach using HBr/BCl3/Ar surface modification followed by Ar physical removal was demonstrated to reduce redeposition and enable atomic‑scale control [Directional atomic layer etching of lithium niobate using Br‑based plasma (arXiv)](https://arxiv.org/html/2511.01825v1)[8].

### Process pressure, DC bias, and substrate temperature
- Pressure and DC bias influence mean free path and ion energy. Lower pressures tend to favor directional (anisotropic) etching; higher DC bias increases ion energy and sputtering that can remove redeposited LiF but can also increase subsurface damage. Empirical optimization of DC bias reduced redeposition while maintaining morphology [Redeposition‑free ICP etching ...](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11501321/)[2].
- Substrate heating (several 100 K) accelerates reaction kinetics and can volatilize or prevent condensation of by‑products; SF6/O2 etching at elevated temperature improved etch rates and surface quality dramatically [The effect of a lithium niobate heating ...](https://cns1.rc.fas.harvard.edu/facilities/docs/The%20effect%20of%20a%20lithium%20niobate%20heating%20on%20the%20etching%20rate%20in%20SF6%20ICP%20plasma.pdf)[6].

## Material and mask strategies to prevent damage
### Mask materials and geometries
- Hard metal masks (Ti/Al/Cr stacks, electroplated Ni) deliver high selectivity and minimize micro‑masking; electroplated nickel masks have reported high selectivity enabling deep etches with reduced redeposition problems [Advanced Etching Techniques ...](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10609314/)[1], [Etching of lithium niobate: From Ridge Waveguides ...](https://www.ecio-conference.org/wp-content/uploads/2016/05/2008/2008_WeD3.pdf)[13].
- SiO2 masks can provide very high etch rates in some ICP recipes (e.g., ~108 nm/min reported) but sometimes at the cost of poorer sidewall angles and selectivity — mask choice must be matched to chemistry and required aspect ratio [Advanced Etching Techniques ...](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10609314/)[1].
- Mask profile: intentionally trapezoidal or re‑entrant profiles can reduce micro‑masking/redeposition effects during deep etches [Redeposition‑free ICP ...](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11501321/)[2].

### Protective coatings and temporary layers
- Diamond‑like carbon (DLC) and other hard, inert coatings have been proposed as protective layers and for improved process stability in PIC manufacture; DLC offers mechanical robustness and etch resistance in some stacks but must be compatible with downstream optical requirements [High density lithium niobate photonic integrated circuits](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41467-023-40502-8)[11].
- Thin conformal ALD oxides or nitrides can serve as sacrificial protective layers against ion damage in some workflows, but care is required because they affect selectivity and mask lifetime.

### Proton exchange and other pre‑treatments
- Proton‑exchanged (PE) LN (where Li+ is partially replaced by H+) shows reduced lithium concentration at the surface, which mitigates LiF redeposition during fluorine etching and can produce near‑vertical sidewalls with appropriate CHF3/Ar ICP recipes (reported ~5.7 µm/h etch rate at 6 mTorr and 130 V dc bias on PE samples) [Plasma etching of proton‑exchanged lithium niobate](https://pubs.aip.org/avs/jva/article/24/4/1012/102827/Plasma-etching-of-proton-exchanged-lithium-niobate)[7], [High‑Quality Dry Etching ... assisted by Proton Substitution](https://www.mdpi.com/2079-4991/12/16/2836)[4].
- Proton exchange can, however, alter optical and ferroelectric properties if not reversed/annealed post‑processing; use when compatible with device design.

## Post‑etch cleaning and annealing to repair or remove damage
### Wet chemical treatments
- Acid rinses: LiF residues and crystalline particles formed after CF4 or other fluorine etching can be removed by HNO3 rinses; heat treatment in O2 can further oxidize and remove LiF, leaving LiNb3O8 transiently in some chemistries before reformation/repair [Growth of crystalline LiF ...](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/abs/pii/S0022024898000098)[9].
- HF/HNO3 mixtures: Wet etching of Z‑cut LN with HF/HNO3 (chemical smoothing) has been used to fabricate low‑loss Ti‑doped ridge waveguides with reported TE losses down to ~0.3 dB/cm when combined with other processing steps [Etching of Lithium Niobate: From Ridge Waveguides ...](https://www.ecio-conference.org/wp-content/uploads/2016/05/2008/2008_WeD3.pdf)[13].

### SC‑1 and SC‑2 cleaning
- Standard clean 1 (SC‑1, NH4OH + H2O2) removes a surface layer enriched in oxygen vacancies and residual contaminants, enabling successful high‑resolution patterning and better baseline surface quality prior to etch or after damaging steps [Thin film LiNbO3 surface preparation using SC‑1](https://opg.optica.org/ome/abstract.cfm?uri=ome-15-11-2826)[10].

### Thermal anneals and re‑crystallization
- Moderate temperature anneals in oxygen can relieve ion damage, reduce oxygen vacancies, and partially recrystallize near‑surface amorphous zones. Very high temperature treatments (near melting) can reshape and re‑crystallize damaged surface zones, but such processes require careful control to avoid domain disruption and are not always compatible with integrated platforms [Ultra‑smooth processing of lithium niobate ...](https://opg.optica.org/abstract.cfm?uri=ol-49-18-5067)[12], [The effect of a lithium niobate heating ...](https://cns1.rc.fas.harvard.edu/facilities/docs/The%20effect%20of%20a%20lithium%20niobate%20heating%20on%20the%20etching%20rate%20in%20SF6%20ICP%20plasma.pdf)[6].
- High‑temperature reduction treatments followed by wet etching have been shown in hybrid processes to produce smooth, vertical sidewalls with minimal damage for some structures [Advanced Etching Techniques ...](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10609314/)[1].

## Advanced approaches: ALE, hybrid dry/wet flows, and damage‑free strategies
- Directional atomic layer etching (ALE) with alternating surface chemistry and low‑energy physical removal offers atomic‑scale control, reduced redeposition and minimal subsurface damage when optimized; recent directional ALE schemes using HBr/BCl3/Ar followed by Ar removal reduce LiF redeposition and yield high control [Directional atomic layer etching ... (arXiv)](https://arxiv.org/html/2511.01825v1)[8].
- Hybrid processes combining dry etch, high‑temperature reduction (to modify surface stoichiometry), and subsequent wet chemical smoothing have produced nearly damage‑free 90° sidewalls in reported demonstrations [Advanced Etching Techniques ...](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10609314/)[1].
- Redeposition‑free ICP recipes have been developed by simultaneously optimizing bias, pressure, mask stack and gas composition to avoid LiF build‑up, achieving deep, smooth trenches with high verticality [Redeposition‑free ICP etching ...](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11501321/)[2].

## Crystal‑structure and orientation considerations
- Etch rate, sidewall morphology and susceptibility to cracking are strongly orientation dependent. The −Z face often etches faster; +c and y faces show different susceptibilities to pulsed‑plasma and photo‑assisted etching, with the y‑surface more prone to directional etching features and cracking in some doped LN (e.g., Fe‑doped) [Etch Rate Dependence on Crystal Orientation of Lithium Niobate](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/21041126/)[5].
- Mask selection and ion bombardment settings should be adjusted per cut: e.g., metal mask stacks were recommended as best for multiple cuts to avoid micro‑masking and redeposition issues [Advanced Etching Techniques ...](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10609314/)[1].

## Empirical benchmarks and recommended process recipes (practical guidance)
The recommendations below synthesize reported best practices from literature. Exact recipes require lab‑level tuning.

1. Low‑damage, high‑quality waveguides (general recipe)
   - Substrate: thin‑film LNOI or bulk LN — choose crystal cut matching device (Z‑cut common for modulators).
   - Mask: Ti/Al/Cr stack or electroplated Ni for deep etches; SiO2 for some ICP recipes if high etch rate prioritized but verify sidewall profile [Advanced Etching Techniques ...](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10609314/)[1], [Redeposition‑free ICP ...](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11501321/)[2].
   - Plasma: ICP with SF6/O2 or NF3/Ar mixtures; tune O2 fraction to reduce LiF formation. Use moderate chamber pressure and elevated substrate temperature (e.g., several 100 K) to boost volatility of by‑products and improve surface quality [The effect of a lithium niobate heating ...](https://cns1.rc.fas.harvard.edu/facilities/docs/The%20effect%20of%20a%20lithium%20niobate%20heating%20on%20the%20etching%20rate%20in%20SF6%20ICP%20plasma.pdf)[6].
   - Bias/ion energy: increase DC bias sufficiently to sputter/remove redeposited LiF but remain below energies causing excessive subsurface amorphization; literature shows raising bias reduces redeposition in optimized ICP flows [Redeposition‑free ICP ...](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11501321/)[2].
   - Post‑etch: SC‑1 clean, HNO3 rinse to remove residual LiF crystals, then oxygen anneal (moderate temperature) to heal oxygen vacancies [Thin film LiNbO3 surface preparation using SC‑1](https://opg.optica.org/ome/abstract.cfm?uri=ome-15-11-2826)[10], [Growth of crystalline LiF ...](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/abs/pii/S0022024898000098)[9].
   - Expected performance: literature reports near‑vertical sidewalls, etch rates in the range 10s–100 nm/min depending on stack, and low optical losses when combined with proper smoothing (e.g., TE propagation losses down to ~0.3 dB/cm in certain ridge waveguide recipes using HF/HNO3 smoothing) [Etching of Lithium Niobate: From Ridge ...](https://www.ecio-conference.org/wp-content/uploads/2016/05/2008/2008_WeD3.pdf)[13].

2. For minimal redeposition and deepest etches
   - Use redispersion‑free ICP recipes reported in recent studies: optimize chamber pressure, DC bias, and use a trapezoidal or composite metal mask geometry; consider HBr/BCl3 additions or transitioning to ALE for atomic‑control, especially for narrow features [Redeposition‑free ICP ...](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11501321/)[2], [Directional ALE ... (arXiv)](https://arxiv.org/html/2511.01825v1)[8].

3. When working with proton‑exchanged LN
   - PE reduces Li at surface and mitigates LiF redeposition; CHF3/Ar ICP on PE samples produced near‑vertical walls and high etch rates under specific bias/pressure conditions — suitable when device design tolerates PE‑altered surface layers or when subsequent anneal re‑establishes desired optical properties [Plasma etching of proton‑exchanged LN](https://pubs.aip.org/avs/jva/article/24/4/1012/102827/Plasma-etching-of-proton-exchanged-lithium-niobate)[7], [High‑Quality Dry Etching ... assisted by Proton Substitution](https://www.mdpi.com/2079-4991/12/16/2836)[4].

## Theoretical / mechanistic insights that inform mitigation
- LiF formation is driven by the high thermodynamic stability and low volatility of LiF relative to metal fluorides; therefore strategies that avoid forming LiF or remove it (chemical dissolution, oxidation, or sputter removal) are most effective [Advanced Etching Techniques ...](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10609314/)[1], [Growth of crystalline LiF ...](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/abs/pii/S0022024898000098)[9].
- Wulff‑Jaccodine modeling and crystal symmetry considerations explain the observed three‑fold symmetry in etched shapes and the orientation dependence of etch facets; this justifies orientation‑specific process tuning for sidewall quality and to avoid crack‑sensitive surfaces [Etch Rate Dependence on Crystal Orientation ...](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/21041126/)[5].
- ALE and sequential surface‑modification + low‑energy removal follow a chemical‑mechanical logic: a low‑energy modification step forms a chemically modified surface layer that can be removed with minimal subsurface damage by gentle physical sputtering — this reduces the need for high ion energies that cause amorphization [Directional ALE ... (arXiv)](https://arxiv.org/html/2511.01825v1)[8].

## Trade‑offs and practical decision framework
- Etch rate vs damage: higher ion energy and more physical sputtering remove redeposited LiF and increase verticality but increase subsurface damage and optical loss. Use post‑etch thermal/chemical repair if higher ion energies are needed for profile control.
- Mask choice vs fabrication complexity: Ni or metal stacks give best selectivity for deep etches but require additional lithography/plating complexity; SiO2 masks simplify process but can lead to poorer sidewall angles in some chemistries.
- ALE vs ICP: ALE gives best ultimate surface quality and atomic control but is slower and may be less mature for large‑area patterning; ICP is faster and scalable but demands careful chemistry and mask strategy to avoid redeposition.
- Crystal cut sensitivity: adapt recipe to cut; e.g., avoid aggressive pulsed/photonic assisted etches on y‑surface that are crack prone; test and qualify each orientation.

## Outstanding challenges and research opportunities
- Scalable ALE for LN with throughput and uniformity suitable for foundry production remains an active research area [Directional ALE ... (arXiv)](https://arxiv.org/html/2511.01825v1)[8].
- Quantitative models linking ion energy distribution, LiF nucleation kinetics, and mask micro‑geometry to predict redeposition in complex patterns are incomplete; improved diagnostic studies (in situ optical emission, mass spectrometry) are needed [Optical diagnostic of LiNbO3 etching in NF3/Ar ICP plasma: Part I](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/abs/pii/S0924424721006117)[3].
- Integration of post‑etch annealing/repair flows that fully restore ferroelectric/photorefractive performance without degrading waveguide patterns is an ongoing materials engineering challenge [Ultra‑smooth processing ...](https://opg.optica.org/abstract.cfm?uri=ol-49-18-5067)[12].

## Recommendations (concise)
- Start with substrate‑specific qualification: measure etch rates/morphology for the chosen cut (+c, −Z, y) using small test patterns.
- Use ICP with SF6/O2 or NF3/Ar and elevated substrate temperature where compatible; tune DC bias upward enough to reduce LiF redeposition but keep ion energies low enough to limit subsurface amorphization [The effect of ... SF6 ICP](https://cns1.rc.fas.harvard.edu/facilities/docs/The%20effect%20of%20a%20lithium%20niobate%20heating%20on%20the%20etching%20rate%20in%20SF6%20ICP%20plasma.pdf)[6], [Redeposition‑free ICP ...](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11501321/)[2].
- Use robust metal hard masks (Ti/Al/Cr or electroplated Ni) and optimized mask geometry to prevent micro‑masking [Advanced Etching Techniques ...](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10609314/)[1].
- If minimal optical loss is required, include post‑etch SC‑1 cleaning + HNO3 rinse and an oxygen anneal; consider HF/HNO3 chemical smoothing for ridge waveguides where appropriate [Thin film LiNbO3 SC‑1](https://opg.optica.org/ome/abstract.cfm?uri=ome-15-11-2826)[10], [Etching of Lithium Niobate: From Ridge ...](https://www.ecio-conference.org/wp-content/uploads/2016/05/2008/2008_WeD3.pdf)[13].
- For ultimate control on nanoscale features, evaluate directional ALE approaches and proton‑exchange assisted etching when device constraints allow [Directional ALE ... (arXiv)](https://arxiv.org/html/2511.01825v1)[8], [Plasma etching of proton‑exchanged LN](https://pubs.aip.org/avs/jva/article/24/4/1012/102827/Plasma-etching-of-proton-exchanged-lithium-niobate)[7].

## Conclusion
Reducing material damage to LN after plasma etching requires an integrated approach: choose plasma chemistry and ion energy to avoid or remove LiF by‑products; use robust mask stacks and mask geometries to limit micro‑masking; employ substrate heating and oxygen‑containing gases to improve by‑product volatility; and apply post‑etch chemical and thermal repairs (SC‑1, HNO3, oxygen anneals) or advanced processes (ALE, proton exchange) where needed. Empirical studies demonstrate that optimized ICP recipes, proper masks, and post‑etch cleaning can yield near‑vertical, low‑loss structures; emerging approaches (ALE, redispersion‑free ICP flows) promise further improvements. The specific recipe must be tailored to crystal cut, device geometry, and acceptable trade‑offs between throughput and surface quality.

prompt: Write an analysis exploring how historical narratives are being reinterpreted through contemporary political and social lenses. Focus on areas like ideologisation of history, instrumentalisation of the past and efforts to reclaim silenced narratives. Analyze how commemorative practices shape historiography and how historical memory serves current agendas. Please provide relevant examples and scholarly perspectives.
article:
# Reinterpreting the Past: Ideologisation, Instrumentalisation, and the Reclamation of Silenced Narratives

## Executive summary

Contemporary political and social forces actively reshape historical narratives. Three overlapping processes are central: (1) ideologisation of history — where historical meaning is aligned with an explicit ideological project; (2) instrumentalisation of the past — where selective memory is used tactically to legitimize policies, mobilize supporters, or marginalize opponents; and (3) reclamation of silenced narratives — where activists, scholars, communities, and institutions broaden the historical record to include previously excluded voices. Commemorative practices (monuments, museums, curricula, public days, place-names) are particularly potent: they both reflect and produce dominant historiographical frames, and they are frequently contested sites where present-day agendas are advanced or resisted. The sections below synthesize scholarly perspectives, mechanisms, case studies, and implications for historiography and public life.

## Conceptual framing: why history is always contemporary

History is not a neutral ledger of facts; it is a set of narratives constructed, chosen, and interpreted in specific contexts. Scholarship emphasizes that historical interpretation is shaped by present concerns — revision and reinterpretation are inherent to the discipline ([Ideology and history](https://www.tandfonline.com/doi/full/10.1080/13569310500395859) [2]; [All History is Revisionist](https://www.neh.gov/article/all-history-revisionist-history) [3]). Public memory scholarship treats remembering as a social and political process: what a society commemorates signals collective identity and power relations ([Public Memory: The Politics of Remembering and Forgetting](https://cdr.lib.unc.edu/downloads/rj430k252?locale=en) [7]).

Key distinctions:
- Ideologisation: embedding past narratives within coherent ideological frameworks to shape identity and loyalty.
- Instrumentalisation: tactical use of selective memory (facts emphasized, omitted, or reframed) for political ends.
- Reclamation: corrective or restorative projects that center marginalized histories and reshape scholarly and popular historiography.

## Ideologisation of history: mechanisms and contemporary examples

Ideologisation connects historical narratives to an explicit program of political meaning-making. Mechanisms include selective curriculum design, state-directed celebration/commemoration, official histories and historiography, media framing, and legal/institutional reforms that privilege one narrative over alternatives.

Mechanisms and effects
- Selective emphasis and omission: choosing which episodes, actors, or interpretations count as foundational to national identity ([Ideology and history](https://www.tandfonline.com/doi/full/10.1080/13569310500395859) [2]).
- Institutionalization of memory: laws, state museums, commemoration days, and public monuments embed one official narrative into civic space ([Instrumentalization of history and politicization of public spaces](http://www.usd.cas.cz/wp-content/uploads/plagat-final.pdf) [4]).
- Epistemic consolidation: marginalizing dissenting scholarship and circulating a single “truth” through education and media ([Re-russia analysis of historical politics](https://re-russia.net/en/expertise/0126/) [1]).

Contemporary examples
- Russia (post-2014 and especially since 2022): state-directed narratives present a consolidated historical account used to mobilize loyalty and justify foreign policy, with alternative views portrayed as foreign influence ([Re-russia analysis of historical politics](https://re-russia.net/en/expertise/0126/) [1]).
- Far-right mobilization: far-right parties and movements reframe certain events or periods (e.g., selective readings of national sieges, wartime episodes) to foment exclusionary identity politics and anti-minority sentiment ([The political power of historical narratives — case of Vienna siege use](https://www.aeaweb.org/research/activated-history-sieges-vienna) [not in final list]; parallel studies in Europe show similar tactics — see International IDEA) ([The past is the...present? How interpretations of the past are shaping democracy in Europe](https://www.idea.int/blog/past-thepresent-how-interpretations-past-are-shaping-democracy-europe) [6]).

Scholarly perspectives
- Ideologisation is not limited to authoritarian contexts; democracies also politicize history through curriculum debates and commemorative politics (e.g., classroom battles such as the 1619 Project vs. the 1776 Commission in the United States) ([The Real Battle for the Soul of America: Historical Narratives in Public Schools](https://www.bostonpoliticalreview.org/post/the-real-battle-for-the-soul-of-america-historical-narratives-in-public-schools) [9]).
- Historians stress that contestation over memory is normative: debates expose values and power, and resisting uncritical state narratives is part of scholarly democracy ([AHA statements on federal activities](https://www.historians.org/perspectives-article/aha-statements-responding-to-federal-activities/) [8]).

## Instrumentalisation of the past: strategies, tools, and political outcomes

Instrumentalisation treats the past as a resource to be mobilized. Unlike ideologisation (which builds an integrated worldview), instrumentalisation is often pragmatic — using history to achieve short- or medium-term political aims.

Common strategies
- Symbolic politics: erecting or removing monuments, renaming streets, and staging rituals to send political signals (e.g., asserting continuity, repudiating enemies).
- Educational policy: revising textbooks and syllabi to foreground preferred narratives or downplay uncomfortable ones ([Instrumentalizing the Past, Brill volume](https://www.degruyterbrill.com/document/doi/10.1515/9783110769791/html) [5]).
- Media framing and misinformation: selective analogies and “usable pasts” simplify complex history into lessons that justify current policy ([The History Illusion and misused analogies](https://tpv-96307.medium.com/the-history-illusion-when-misused-analogies-distort-political-judgment-b389e8d8c0b1) [not in final list]).
- Legal measures and censorship: legislation can restrict teaching or public expression about certain historical events.

Political outcomes
- Legitimization: rulers justify policies by invoking historical continuity or existential threats.
- Mobilization: evocative historical symbols trigger emotions (pride, grievance) that increase political engagement.
- Exclusion and marginalization: selected commemorative schemas marginalize groups whose histories are omitted or denigrated.

Illustrative cases
- Post-war Poland: Communist-era manipulation of Auschwitz narratives prioritized antifascist communist triumphs over specific Jewish suffering, reshaping public understanding and serving a partisan memory politics ([Power Structures and Divergent Historical Narratives in Post-Communist Poland — SCU paper](https://scholarcommons.scu.edu/cgi/viewcontent.cgi?article=1198&context=historical-perspectives) [17]).
- Election-time manipulations: fabricated or exaggerated historical claims have been used tactically in electoral contexts (international case-studies summarized in the literature on politics of the past) ([Politics of the Past: The Use and Abuse of History](https://www.socialistsanddemocrats.eu/sites/default/files/2856_EN_politics_past_en_090603_1.pdf) [16]).
- Far-right historical distortion: extremist groups selectively deploy history to normalize exclusionary projects (documented across Europe) ([Radical Histories, Distorted Pasts](https://praticasdahistoria.pt/radical-histories-distorted-pasts-the-far-right-and-the-political-instrumentalisation-of-history) [not in final list]; see broader reviews in Brill volume) ([Instrumentalizing the Past, Brill](https://www.degruyterbrill.com/document/doi/10.1515/9783110769791/html) [5]).

## Reclaiming silenced narratives: methods, actors, and effects on historiography

Reclamation re-centers voices excluded by dominant narratives: enslaved people, colonized peoples, women, disabled communities, Indigenous peoples, LGBTQ+ communities, and others. Methods include archival recovery, oral history, museums and monument redesign, curriculum reform, and digital projects.

Agents and methods
- Grassroots activism and descendant communities: community-led memorial projects, oral-history projects, and demands for reparative commemoration decenter official narratives ([Reclaiming History and Repairing Injustice](https://www.searchablemuseum.com/reclaiming-history-and-repairing-injustice/) [1]).
- Academic revision and inclusive pedagogy: scholars and educators integrate marginalized sources and perspectives into teaching and research ([Inclusive History Education, Historical Thinking](https://uu.diva-portal.org/smash/get/diva2:1975645/FULLTEXT01.pdf) [20]).
- Public-history interventions: museums, archives, and digital platforms (e.g., Reveal Digital) amplify under‑represented records and create accessible resources for community history ([Reveal Digital: Bringing marginalized histories to light](https://about.jstor.org/blog/reveal-digital-bringing-marginalized-histories-to-light-through-crowdfunding/) [19]).
- Commemorative justice and monument reimagining: removal of objectionable monuments is often paired with new memorials, contextual plaques, and community consultations ([The Commemorative Justice Movement — Monument Lab](https://monumentlab.com/bulletin/the-commemorative-justice-movement) [10]).

Effects on historiography
- Broadening of the archive: inclusion of oral testimony, material culture, and nontraditional sources alters research questions and methodologies, producing richer, more complex accounts ([Inclusive archival practices — SAAERS and related literature](https://saaers.wordpress.com/2024/02/29/bridging-historical-gaps-the-importance-of-inclusive-archival-practices/) [not in final list]).
- Reorientation of themes: moving from elite-centered political narratives to social, gender, labor, environmental, and subaltern histories ([Inclusive History Education, Historical Thinking](https://uu.diva-portal.org/smash/get/diva2:1975645/FULLTEXT01.pdf) [20]).
- Challenge to epistemic authority: democratizing who can produce historical knowledge — universities, community historians, and digital projects all participate ([Reveal Digital](https://about.jstor.org/blog/reveal-digital-bringing-marginalized-histories-to-light-through-crowdfunding/) [19]; [Making Black history matter in public space — Brookings](https://www.brookings.edu/articles/making-black-history-matter-in-public-space/) [11]).

Case examples
- Black public history and monuments in the US: campaigns to erect memorials to enslaved people and to reinterpret existing monuments are accompanied by curricular and museum changes that redirect public understanding of national foundations ([Making Black history matter in public space — Brookings](https://www.brookings.edu/articles/making-black-history-matter-in-public-space/) [11]).
- Disability history: centering disability movements (e.g., ADA activism) changes narratives about citizenship and rights in U.S. history ([Disability History and the Disability Rights Movement — NPS summary](https://www.nps.gov/articles/disabilityhistoryrightsmovement.htm) [not in final list]).
- Digital recovery projects: crowd-funded digitization projects and AI-enabled discovery are surfacing previously inaccessible materials that reshape local and national histories ([Reveal Digital bringing marginalized histories to light](https://about.jstor.org/blog/reveal-digital-bringing-marginalized-histories-to-light-through-crowdfunding/) [19]; [Uncovering Historical Silences with AI](https://www.historica.org/blog/ai-unexpected-role-in-uncovering-historical-silences) [not in final list]).

## Commemorative practices as drivers of historiography

Commemoration is both an index of historiographical priorities and a tool that shapes future historiography.

How commemoration influences historiography
- Material anchors of memory: monuments and museum exhibits create visible, enduring narratives that structure civic knowledge and academic inquiry ([Commemorative Artefactual Speech](https://journals.publishing.umich.edu/ergo/article/id/7962/) [not in final list]; [Public Memory: The Politics of Remembering and Forgetting](https://cdr.lib.unc.edu/downloads/rj430k252?locale=en) [7]).
- Curriculum feedback loops: what is commemorated publicly often appears in textbooks and classroom teaching, reinforcing certain research agendas and silences ([AHA statements; education debates over 1619 Project vs 1776 Commission](https://www.historians.org/perspectives-article/aha-statements-responding-to-federal-activities/) [8]; [The Real Battle for the Soul of America](https://www.bostonpoliticalreview.org/post/the-real-battle-for-the-soul-of-america-historical-narratives-in-public-schools) [9]).
- Contestation stimulates research: conflicts over monuments and memory prompt scholarly inquiry, new archival work, and public history projects that revise prior accounts ([Marginalisation through commemoration: Trends and practices](https://www.tandfonline.com/doi/full/10.1080/07292473.2020.1786891) [14]; [The Commemorative Justice Movement — Monument Lab](https://monumentlab.com/bulletin/the-commemorative-justice-movement) [10]).

Examples of commemorative contestation shaping historiography
- Confederate monuments debate (U.S.): removal and reinterpretation led to a surge in scholarship on the “Lost Cause,” race, memory, and public history practice. Monument removals prompted new local history work and museum exhibits documenting slavery and Jim Crow ([Marginalisation through commemoration](https://www.tandfonline.com/doi/full/10.1080/07292473.2020.1786891) [14]).
- Auschwitz memory: disputes about how to represent multiple victim groups and the political uses of the site drove international scholarly debate about Holocaust memory and the politics of memorialization in post-authoritarian states ([Power Structures and Divergent Historical Narratives in Post-Communist Poland — SCU paper](https://scholarcommons.scu.edu/cgi/viewcontent.cgi?article=1198&context=historical-perspectives) [17]).
- National curriculum contests: battles over how to teach slavery, colonialism, and national founding narratives have affected historiographical priorities and funding for related research ([The Real Battle for the Soul of America](https://www.bostonpoliticalreview.org/post/the-real-battle-for-the-soul-of-america-historical-narratives-in-public-schools) [9]).

## Scholarly debates and interdisciplinary perspectives

Key scholarly tensions
- Neutrality vs. engagement: some argue scholarship should remain dispassionate to preserve credibility; others contend that historians have civic responsibilities and should engage with present injustices ([The best scholarship is political but with no ideological stamp — Times Higher Education](https://www.timeshighereducation.com/blog/best-scholarship-political-no-ideological-stamp) [not in final list]).
- Revisionism as method vs. propagandistic revisionism: historians view revisionism as essential to the discipline, but the same techniques can serve propagandistic ends when applied without rigorous methods ([All History is Revisionist — NEH](https://www.neh.gov/article/all-history-revisionist-history) [3]; [Paradoxes of historical revisionism in authoritarian states — literature overview](https://onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/full/10.1080/25739638.2025.2489261) [18]).
- Public scholarship and memory studies: interdisciplinary work (history, political science, sociology, rhetoric, cultural studies) enriches the study of commemoration and the politics of memory ([Narrative and social movements — Polletta](https://sites.socsci.uci.edu/~polletta/Articles%20and%20Book%20Chapters_files/polletta%20chen%20narrative%20and%20social%20movements.pdf) [12]; [Public Memory scholarship — Berkeley belonging overview](https://belonging.berkeley.edu/power-and-promise-public-memory) [15]).

Methodological advances
- Expanded archives and methods: oral history, crowdsourced digitization, material culture analysis, and computational tools (including AI) are broadening evidence bases and enabling revisionist and corrective projects ([Reveal Digital](https://about.jstor.org/blog/reveal-digital-bringing-marginalized-histories-to-light-through-crowdfunding/) [19]; [Inclusive History Education, Historical Thinking](https://uu.diva-portal.org/smash/get/diva2:1975645/FULLTEXT01.pdf) [20]).
- Narrative analysis in political mobilization: social-movement scholarship shows how narrative frames convert private grievances into public action; this applies to both state instrumentalisation and grassroots reclamation ([Polletta — narrative and social movements](https://sites.socsci.uci.edu/~polletta/Articles%20and%20Book%20Chapters_files/polletta%20chen%20narrative%20and%20social%20movements.pdf) [12]).

## Policy implications and strategies to strengthen historiographical integrity

Policy and civic recommendations
- Protect scholarly independence: legal and institutional safeguards for historiography and academic freedom reduce the risk of state-directed myths ([AHA statements on federal activities](https://www.historians.org/perspectives-article/aha-statements-responding-to-federal-activities/) [8]).
- Invest in inclusive archives and public-history infrastructure: funding digitization, community archiving, and inclusive museum practice expands the evidence base and democratizes historical knowledge ([Reveal Digital](https://about.jstor.org/blog/reveal-digital-bringing-marginalized-histories-to-light-through-crowdfunding/) [19]; [Inclusive History Education, Historical Thinking](https://uu.diva-portal.org/smash/get/diva2:1975645/FULLTEXT01.pdf) [20]).
- Promote critical history education: curricula that teach historical thinking, source evaluation, and contested memory prepare citizens to recognize instrumentalisation ([Inclusive History Education](https://uu.diva-portal.org/smash/get/diva2:1975645/FULLTEXT01.pdf) [20]; [Public Memory: The Politics of Remembering and Forgetting](https://cdr.lib.unc.edu/downloads/rj430k252?locale=en) [7]).
- Use participatory commemoration: public consultations, pluralistic monuments, and contestatory plaques allow multiple perspectives in civic landscapes (models from the Commemorative Justice movement) ([The Commemorative Justice Movement — Monument Lab](https://monumentlab.com/bulletin/the-commemorative-justice-movement) [10]).

Risks and trade-offs
- Politicized curriculum reforms and top-down commemorative projects can exacerbate polarization if implemented without broad civic input ([The Real Battle for the Soul of America](https://www.bostonpoliticalreview.org/post/the-real-battle-for-the-soul-of-america-historical-narratives-in-public-schools) [9]).
- Counter-reform efforts can be co-opted or instrumentalized by new actors; inclusive projects require sustained institutional support and community leadership.

## Conclusion

Historical narratives are continually reconstructed to serve present-day meanings: ideologisation and instrumentalisation can consolidate power and exclude, while reclamation efforts open archives, broaden perspectives, and contest dominant memories. Commemorative practices are central—both as instruments of political strategy and as sites of contestation that shape historiography. Strengthening scholarly independence, investing in inclusive archival and educational infrastructures, and ensuring participatory commemoration are key to preventing abusive uses of the past and to cultivating a plural, evidence-based public history.
