article:
# Manufacturing technology options for hollow motor shafts in NEV electric drive units — comprehensive review

## Executive summary
Hollow motor shafts for New Energy Vehicle (NEV) electric drive units are manufactured today using a range of forming and fabrication routes. The dominant families are: (A) tube-based machining and deep-hole boring from seamless tube, (B) near-net-shape bulk forming (forging, radial/rotary forging, cold forging, rotary swaging, pilgering), (C) extrusion (mainly aluminium hollow sections), (D) casting for complex geometries or lower-strength parts, (E) welding/seam-join of fabricated tube sections, and (F) additive-manufacturing or composite routes for low-volume or highly optimized lightweight designs. Each route has distinct trade-offs in material compatibility, cost at volume, mechanical performance (fatigue, strength), required downstream operations (heat treatment, spline broaching, grinding, balancing), scrap and cycle time.

Recommended primary manufacturing routes for NEV electric drive hollow shafts:
- For high-volume, high-strength steel shafts: near-net radial/closed-die forging or cold forging of hollow preforms (seamless tube), followed by precise turning/grinding, spline broaching or broach-rolling, heat treatment (quench & temper or nitriding) and dynamic balancing. This balances fatigue performance, strength and cost per part at scale [Evaluation of EV Hollow Shaft - Shimadzu][10], [Hollow Shaft Forging (manufacturers)][17], [US9446445B2][5].
- For medium-volume/high-precision shafts: precision machining from seamless tube (deep-hole boring, mill-turn, grinding) with heat treatment and surface hardening — lower tooling capital than forging, higher cycle time and scrap but greater flexibility and tight tolerances [Motor Shaft Machining guides][8][16].
- For lightweight aluminium shafts where strength requirements are moderate: precision extrusion plus CNC finishing and surface treatment; useful for weight-sensitive subassemblies or non-rotor drive components but limited for very high-speed/high-stress rotor shafts [Aluminium extrusions for powertrains][6], [Extrusion in commercial vehicle manufacturing][7].
- For highly optimized ultra-light solutions or small production runs: rotary swaging / pilger + heat treatment or metal additive manufacturing for complex internal features — promising but currently niche for traction shafts due to cost, qualification and fatigue life concerns [Rotary swaging research][9], [Case studies on process change][18].

Key downstream needs regardless of forming route: spline/gear feature generation (broaching, hobbing or rolling), final OD/ID grinding or honing for bearing fits, precision balancing, heat treatment (quench/temper or surface hardening like nitriding), and non-destructive inspection to meet NVH and safety requirements [Machining and post-process guidance][8][16].

## Functional and NEV-specific requirements for hollow motor shafts
NEV traction motor shafts have stricter combined requirements compared with generic shafts. Typical requirements that drive manufacturing choice include:
- High fatigue strength at elevated rotational speeds (high rpm), especially for rotor shafts and input/output shafts of e-axles.
- Tight geometric tolerances for bearings, couplings and gear/spline interfaces (typical concentricity, runout and surface finish requirements).
- Low mass (improved specific power and vehicle range) while retaining stiffness and torsional strength.
- NVH (noise, vibration, harshness) driven dynamic balance and surface integrity requirements.
- High dimensional repeatability for automated assembly lines (IATF16949 production).
- Cost-effectiveness at anticipated production volumes (tens of thousands to millions per year for mainstream EVs).
These requirements favor processes that produce good fatigue properties, predictable grain flow and allow economical finishing of bearing journals and spline features [Motor shaft and NEV reports][11][16].

## Forming and fabrication techniques — descriptions and applicability
Each process below is described, followed by material suitability, typical finishing steps, cost-volume suitability, advantages and limitations.

### 1) Precision machining from solid or from seamless tube (turning, deep-hole boring, milling, grinding, EDM)
Description: Conventional subtractive manufacturing using CNC lathes, mill-turn centers, deep-hole drilling/boring to form ID, OD, bores and features. Final grinding/honing ensures bearing fits; EDM or broaching for internal splines. Common for prototypes, low-medium volumes and high-precision parts [Motor Shaft Machining guides][8][16].

- Suitable materials: carbon steels (e.g., 1045, 4140), alloy steels (4140/4340), stainless steels, titanium, aluminium.
- Typical downstream steps: heat treatment (quench & temper, nitriding), precision grinding, broaching/broach-rolling of splines, dynamic balancing, surface finishing/coating.
- Cost-effectiveness: economical for low-to-medium volumes and when flexibility needed; per-part machining cost remains high for heavy material removal and long cycle times.
- Pros: excellent precision, flexibility to change designs, minimal process qualification for variants.
- Cons: high material waste (especially if machining from solid), longer cycle time, higher per-piece cost at volume.
- Sources: [Motor Shaft Machining guide][8], [HMaking machining services][16].

### 2) Near-net-shape bulk forging (radial forging, closed-die forging, mandrel/rotary forging)
Description: Deformation-based shaping of hollow shafts from billets or tubes to refine grain flow, reduce stock removal and improve mechanical properties. Radial forging (or rotary radial forging) and closed-die forging for hollow geometries have been used in EV shaft production to raise fatigue life while reducing weight and machining [Evaluation of EV Hollow Shaft - Shimadzu][10], [Hollow shaft forging suppliers][17].

- Suitable materials: alloy steels (4140, 4340), carbon steels, some stainless steels.
- Typical downstream steps: finish machining of journals and splines, heat treatment (quench & temper), grinding, balancing.
- Cost-effectiveness: high initial tooling cost but low per-part cost at high volumes; significant material and machining time savings compared with full machining from solid [Case study: cost reduction by switching to cold forging][18].
- Pros: improved mechanical properties (grain flow), reduced machining allowance, high throughput when amortized; good for high-strength, fatigue-critical parts.
- Cons: high tooling investment, longer lead time for tool development, complexity in achieving precise internal features (may need mandrels or subsequent drilling).
- Sources: [Shimadzu radial forging evaluation][10], [US9446445B2 method for hollow shafts][5], [Hollow shaft forging supplier pages][17].

### 3) Cold forging / cold upset / cold extrusion from tube (including rotary swaging)
Description: Cold forming processes that reshape tube preforms to near-final geometry. Rotary swaging reduces diameter and can create complex stepped profiles. Cold forging improves strength via work hardening and favorable grain orientation [Rotary swaging research][9], [Case examples][18].

- Suitable materials: low-to-medium alloy steels, some stainless steels; aluminium alloys for extrusion/swaging variants.
- Typical downstream steps: stress relief or tempering (if needed), finish machining, surface hardening/nitriding for wear surfaces, balancing.
- Cost-effectiveness: very good for high volumes; tooling costs moderate; shorter cycle times than hot forging in many cases.
- Pros: excellent material utilization, improved fatigue by work hardening and refined microstructure, can produce long shafts economically.
- Cons: limited to geometry changes achievable cold; higher forming loads and possible springback; some steels require intermediate heat treatments.
- Sources: [Rotary swaging lightweight manufacturing][9], [cold-forging case study][18].

### 4) Pilgering / tube drawing / tube rolling (seamless tube forming)
Description: Produces thin-walled high-integrity seamless tubes (pilger rolling, tube drawing) used as starting material for hollow shafts. Subsequent machining yields final features.

- Suitable materials: alloy steels, stainless steels.
- Typical downstream: machining of ends and features, heat treatment, finishing.
- Cost-effectiveness: efficient when the main geometry is a tube; low material waste; requires supply chain for high-quality seamless tube.
- Pros: produces high-quality seamless sections with good mechanical properties and dimensional control.
- Cons: requires subsequent machining for complex features; tube procurement may be limiting for short lead times.

### 5) Extrusion (direct and hollow-section extrusion) — mainly aluminium
Description: Continuous or billet extrusion to create hollow profiles with constant cross-section. Commonly used for aluminium hollow members in BEV powertrains for lightweighting [Aluminium extrusions for powertrains][6], [Extrusion in commercial vehicle manufacturing][7].

- Suitable materials: aluminium alloys (6xxx series), some low-strength copper alloys.
- Typical downstream: CNC machining of flanges, journals and bearing seats, heat treatment (T6 for aluminium), surface treatment/anodizing, balancing.
- Cost-effectiveness: excellent for parts with constant cross-sections and high volumes; tooling (dies) cost moderate.
- Pros: lightweight, corrosion resistant, excellent material utilization for long profiles.
- Cons: limited to lower-strength materials — not ideal for high-stress rotor shafts unless reinforced; less suitable for complex variable cross-section shafts.

### 6) Casting (investment casting, die casting)
Description: Molten metal cast into molds—investment or precision casting for complex internal/external shapes; die casting for aluminium shapes.

- Suitable materials: aluminium (die casting), cast steels and irons for lower-stress components.
- Typical downstream: heat treatment, CNC finishing, machining of critical surfaces, surface treatment.
- Cost-effectiveness: viable for complex geometries that are difficult to machine; lower mechanical properties than forged/forged-and-machined parts for high-cycle fatigue parts.
- Pros: low-cost for complex shapes, minimal machining for some geometries.
- Cons: porosity, lower fatigue strength, not preferable for high-speed rotor shafts subject to cyclic fatigue.

### 7) Welded/fabricated tube assemblies (seam-welded tubes, multi-piece assemblies)
Description: Fabrication by welding machined components or seam-welding rolled tubes, then finish-machining mounts and journals.

- Suitable materials: carbon and alloy steels, stainless steels, aluminium.
- Downstream: heavy finishing and post-weld heat treatment, dynamic balancing.
- Cost-effectiveness: lower tooling cost for low volumes or large diameter shafts; welded joints reduce fatigue life if not carefully controlled.
- Pros: flexible for complex internal architectures or large diameters.
- Cons: welds are high-risk fatigue locations; often require reinforcement and strict NDT.

### 8) Additive manufacturing (metal AM, directed energy deposition) and composites (filament winding, mandrel removal)
Description: Metal AM (SLM, DED) can produce shafts with internal cooling channels or complex features; composite hollow shafts are made by filament winding around a mandrel, followed by curing and mandrel removal.

- Suitable materials: stainless steels, titanium and high-strength aluminium alloys (AM); carbon or glass fiber composites for composite shafts.
- Typical downstream: machining of bearing journals, surface finishing, nondestructive exam; composites often need metallic end fittings that are bonded or co-cured.
- Cost-effectiveness: currently high per-piece cost; suitable for prototyping, low-volume premium applications or highly optimized lightweight designs.
- Pros: internal complexity, integration of cooling channels, potential mass reduction.
- Cons: certification, repeatability, fatigue life and NVH qualification challenges for traction shafts; limited industrial adoption for high-cycle drivetrain parts [Additive/composite literature][3][13].

## Comparison matrix — practical criteria
A decision-oriented comparison is provided below (relative ratings: High / Medium / Low). "Scale" indicates suitability by production volume.

- Precision machining from tube
  - Material compatibility: High (steels, stainless, aluminium)
  - Mechanical performance (fatigue, strength): High (after heat treatment)
  - Cost per part: Medium–High (low volumes acceptable)
  - Tooling/CapEx: Low–Medium
  - Lead time to production: Short–Medium
  - Post-processing needs: Extensive (grinding, broaching, heat treatment, balancing)
  - Scale: Low–Medium volumes
  - Sources: [Motor Shaft Machining][8], [HMaking][16]

- Near-net forging (radial/closed-die)
  - Material compatibility: High (alloy & carbon steels)
  - Mechanical performance: Very High (improved grain flow, fatigue)
  - Cost per part: Low at high volumes
  - Tooling/CapEx: High
  - Lead time: Longer (tooling design)
  - Post-processing: Finish machining + heat treat + grinding + balancing
  - Scale: Medium–High volumes
  - Sources: [Shimadzu radial forging][10], [US9446445B2][5]

- Cold forging / rotary swaging
  - Material compatibility: Medium–High (suitable alloys)
  - Mechanical performance: High (work hardening improves properties)
  - Cost per part: Low at high volumes
  - Tooling/CapEx: Medium
  - Lead time: Medium
  - Post-processing: Light-to-moderate machining, heat treat possible
  - Scale: Medium–High
  - Sources: [Rotary swaging research][9], [cold-forging case][18]

- Extrusion (aluminium)
  - Material compatibility: High for aluminium; low for high-strength steel needs
  - Mechanical performance: Medium (aluminium has lower fatigue strength than alloy steels)
  - Cost per part: Low–Medium for high volumes
  - Tooling/CapEx: Medium (dies)
  - Lead time: Medium
  - Post-processing: CNC finishing, heat treatment, anodizing
  - Scale: Medium–High
  - Sources: [LightMetalAge aluminium extrusions][6], [Kimsen extrusion use][7]

- Casting
  - Material compatibility: High (aluminium, iron, some steels)
  - Mechanical performance: Low–Medium (porosity & lower fatigue)
  - Cost per part: Low for complex geometry and medium volumes
  - Tooling/CapEx: Medium–High (molds/dies)
  - Lead time: Medium
  - Post-processing: CNC finishing, heat treat
  - Scale: Medium
  - Sources: Driveshaft/casting general info [14]

- Welded/fabricated tube
  - Material compatibility: High (various)
  - Mechanical performance: Medium–Low (weld fatigue is concern)
  - Cost per part: Medium (depends on labor automation)
  - Tooling/CapEx: Low–Medium
  - Lead time: Short–Medium
  - Post-processing: Extensive inspection and heat treatment
  - Scale: Low–Medium

- Additive manufacturing / composites
  - Material compatibility: Medium (AM steels/titanium; composites: CFRP)
  - Mechanical performance: Medium–High (composites high specific stiffness; AM material properties vary)
  - Cost per part: High (currently)
  - Tooling/CapEx: Low tooling but high equipment cost
  - Lead time: Short for prototypes
  - Post-processing: Significant for machined interfaces, qualification
  - Scale: Low (prototyping, niche)
  - Sources: composite and AM reviews [3][13]

## Typical downstream processing requirements (independent of forming route)
- Heat treatment: quench & temper for alloy steels, nitriding/carburizing for surface wear resistance, stress relieving for cold-formed parts [Material and heat-treatment guidance][15].
- Precision machining: OD/ID grinding, journal finish grinding, spline broaching/hobbing or roll forming for splines [Machining guides][8][16].
- Dynamic balancing: mandatory for rotor and high-speed shafts to meet NVH specs.
- Non-destructive testing: ultrasonic or magnetic particle inspection for forged/welded parts; dimensional inspection via CMM.
- Surface treatment: coatings, anodizing (aluminium), plating or shot-peening to boost fatigue [Material guides][15].
- Assembly operations: shrink-fit or press-fit assembly, keyways or spline integration; some designs replace press-fit with shrink-fitting to reduce stresses [Design case studies][18].

## Material considerations — selection mapped to processes
- Alloy steels (4140, 4340) — preferred for high-strength, high-fatigue critical shafts; compatible with forging, cold forming and machining; respond well to quench & temper and nitriding [Material guides][15].
- Carbon steels (1045, 1018) — economical, machinable; can be used where extreme strength is not required.
- Stainless steels (17-4PH, 316) — chosen where corrosion resistance required; 17-4PH offers good strength and can be precipitation hardened (used in some drivetrain components).
- Aluminium alloys — excellent for lightweight designs via extrusion and machining; limited for high-speed rotor shafts unless the design tolerates lower strength and uses larger diameters or reinforcements [Aluminium extrusions][6].
- Titanium and nickel alloys — niche due to cost; used where high strength-to-weight and environment resistance are mandated.
- Composites (CFRP) — very low mass and high specific stiffness; joining to metallic interfaces and fatigue qualification are challenges; more common in driveshafts than rotor shafts today [Composite reviews][13].

## Process selection decision guide (practical)
Select process based on these prioritized constraints:

1. Performance (fatigue/strength) highest priority → choose forging (radial/closed-die) or cold-forged tube followed by heat treatment and finish machining [Shimadzu evaluation][10].
2. Tightest dimensional tolerances and low batch-size / design changes → select precision machining from seamless tube and high-accuracy grinding/broach operations [Motor Shaft Machining][8].
3. Lowest mass with moderate structural loads and high volumes → aluminium extrusion + CNC finishing, T6 treating and surface protection [LightMetalAge aluminium extrusions][6].
4. Large production quantities and low per-part cost targets → invest in forming tooling (forging or cold forming) to reduce machining time and material waste [Cost-efficient selection studies][11].
5. Complex internal features (cooling channels, integrated cavities) → consider AM or multi-piece assembly; note qualification and cost challenges [AM/composite literature][3].

## Recommended manufacturing routes for NEV electric drive hollow shafts (practical flows)
The following are recommended process flows tailored to typical NEV use-cases.

1) High-performance traction rotor or input shaft (steel, high rpm, high fatigue resistance) — recommended route:
   - Start: precision seamless alloy steel tube or forged hollow preform.
   - Forming: radial forging / closed-die forging or cold forging/rotary swaging to near-net shape [Shimadzu][10].
   - Heat treat: quench & temper.
   - Finish machining: OD/ID turning, precision grinding for bearing journals; broaching/roll-forming for splines.
   - Surface hardening: nitriding or shot-peening.
   - Final: dynamic balancing, NDT and CMM inspection.
   - Rationale: delivers best fatigue life and lowest machining allowance at volume [US9446445B2][5], [Shimadzu][10].

2) Medium-volume precision shaft (limited tooling budget, high geometric accuracy):
   - Start: high-quality seamless tube.
   - Machining: mill-turn deep-hole boring for internal diameter, CNC turning for journals, broaching for splines.
   - Heat treat: quench & temper or nitriding.
   - Finish: grinding/honing, balancing, inspection.
   - Rationale: flexibility, short lead time, high precision albeit higher per-part cost [Motor Shaft Machining][8].

3) Lightweight secondary shafts or housings (aluminium, medium stress):
   - Start: aluminium extrusion (hollow).
   - Forming: extrusion to near profile, billet machining of features.
   - Heat treatment: solution and ageing (T6), surface anodizing.
   - Finish: machining of bearing journals and mounting features, balancing.
   - Rationale: best weight savings for moderate-load applications; lower fatigue compared to steel so restricted to appropriate positions [LightMetalAge][6].

4) Niche optimized shafts (low volume, complex internal channels):
   - AM (DED/SLM) or composite filament winding with metallic end fittings.
   - Post: finish-machining mating surfaces, rigorous testing and qualification.
   - Rationale: enables complex internal geometry (cooling), but high cost and long qualification cycles [AM/composite sources][3][13].

## Cost considerations and examples
- Tooling capex for forging/cold-forming is high but amortized at scale; switching from machining to forging can reduce part cost, scrap and machine hours significantly (case studies report up to ~35–40% production cost reduction after re-design and process change) [Turnkey machining & redesign case studies][1][18].
- Machining-dominated routes have lower capex but higher unit material removal and cycle time; economical for prototyping and lower volumes [Machining guides][8][16].
- Extrusions require moderate die costs and are cost-effective where geometry is constant and volumes are high [LightMetalAge][6].
- Adopting near-net processes reduces machining time and material waste; radial forging specifically showed improved microstructure and weight reductions in EV shaft trials [Shimadzu radial forging][10].

## Risks, qualification and manufacturing controls
- Forged/cold-formed parts require robust tooling design and process control to avoid in-die defects; NDT protocols must be in place for fatigue-critical parts [US9446445B2][5].
- Welded/fabricated designs carry fatigue risk at welds and require post-weld heat treatment and stringent inspection.
- AM/composite routes require extensive qualification for fatigue life, interface durability and NVH behavior before fleet deployment.
- All routes must integrate dynamic balancing, CMM-based dimensional control, and part traceability to meet automotive quality standards (IATF 16949).

## Final recommendations (concise)
- For mainstream NEV traction shafts (highest performance + cost sensitivity): adopt near-net forging (radial/closed-die) or cold-forging/rotary swaging from seamless tube combined with controlled heat treatment, finish machining and surface hardening. This optimizes strength, fatigue life and unit cost at production scale [Shimadzu][10], [US9446445B2][5].
- For lower-volume or rapidly changing designs: use precision machining from high-quality seamless tube with deep-hole techniques and CNC mill-turn centers for tolerance-critical features [Motor Shaft Machining][8].
- For lightweight secondary shafts: use aluminium extrusion + finishing where mechanical load permits [LightMetalAge][6].
- Maintain process qualification plans, controlled heat-treatment and post-process NVH balancing for any chosen route.

### Sources
[1] Efficient Turnkey Machining of Complex e-Drive Components: https://cti-symposium.world/efficient-turnkey-machining-of-complex-e-drive-components/

[2] Hollow drive shaft for vehicle and manufacturing method (US20160305469A1): https://patents.google.com/patent/US20160305469A1/en

[3] The Engineering Behind Hollow Shaft Motors — EMP Drives blog: https://www.empdrives.com/blog/the-engineering-behind-hollow-shaft-motors-everything-you-need-to-know/

[4] HOLLOW SHAFT｜NEW TECHNOLOGY｜KANETA KOGYO CO., LTD.: https://www.kanetakogyo.co.jp/en/latest_technology/hollow_shaft/

[5] Method for manufacturing hollow shafts (US9446445B2): https://patents.google.com/patent/US9446445B2/en

[6] Aluminum Extrusions for All Automotive Powertrains — Light Metal Age: https://www.lightmetalage.com/news/industry-news/extrusion/aluminum-extrusions-for-all-automotive-powertrains/

[7] The use of extrusion technology in commercial vehicle manufacturing — Kimsen: https://kimsen.vn/the-use-of-extrusion-technology-in-commercial-vehicle-manufacturing-ne133.html

[8] Motor Shaft Machining: A Complete Technical Guide — Topsbest Precision: https://topsbest-precision.com/blog/motor-shaft-machining/

[11] Cost-efficient selection of manufacturing technologies for an electric traction motor shaft — Fraunhofer (publica): https://publica.fraunhofer.de/bitstreams/a343908c-8dd5-4ed6-bcbf-366b0a2a9d09/download

What methods can be employed to enhance the actual control performance of PID algorithms, and how should PID parameters be optimally selected?
article:
# Improving PID control performance for UAVs across varying flight conditions

## Executive summary
PID-based cascaded controllers remain the dominant architecture in small- and medium-size UAVs because of simplicity and low compute cost, but a single fixed PID gain set rarely performs well across wide flight envelopes (hover, cruise, aggressive maneuvers, variable payload, turbulence). Practical improvement requires a combination of (a) better baseline tuning and loop design (filters, anti-windup, sampling), (b) offline optimization and model-based/system-identification tuning, and (c) online adaptation (gain-scheduling, self‑tuning, fuzzy/NN augmentation or learning-based tuning) plus safety supervisory measures. Hybrid strategies (well‑tuned baseline PID + online adaptive layer + conservative safety/fallback gains) give the best trade-off between performance, robustness and certification/validation cost. The sections below summarize methods, evidence from literature, practical recipes for selecting and updating gains, implementation guidance, and recommended workflows.

## Background: why single-set PID fails in varied flight states
- Multirotor dynamics are strongly nonlinear and vary with flight condition, speed, payload and environment (wind/turbulence). Classical linear PID implicitly assumes near-linear plant behaviour and fixed disturbance characteristics, so gains optimized for one condition (e.g., light hover) will underperform in others (e.g., fast forward flight or heavy payload) [1] [PID control of quadrotor UAVs: A survey](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/abs/pii/S1367578823000640), [2] [PID Control and Alternative Control Approaches in UAV Systems](https://www.preprints.org/manuscript/202509.1583/v1/download).
- Typical failure modes from mismatched gains: excessive oscillation (aggressive Kp or Kd), slow response / steady-state error (low Kp/Ki), actuator saturation and integral windup, degraded disturbance rejection during gusts, and poor tracking at high speed [6] [PID tuning principles guide](https://theuavtech.com/wp-content/uploads/2020/10/UAV-Tech-PID-Tuning-Principles.pdf), [1] [PID control survey](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/abs/pii/S1367578823000640).

## Methodologies to improve PID performance (summary and evidence)
The literature and field practice group methods into offline design/tuning, runtime adaptation, hybrid/learning-based augmentation, and engineering-level loop improvements.

### 1) Offline modeling, system identification and optimization
- System identification (linear models at specific operating points) allows using model-based tuning methods (loop-shaping, H2/H∞ objectives) or generating multiple gain sets for gain-scheduling. Iterative Feedback Tuning (IFT) and cascade IFT minimize closed-loop performance cost using measured input-output data without explicit full model identification [10] [An iterative feedback tuning scheme for multiloop PID](https://luisbgz.com/wp-content/publications/Ramirez_2010_An_iterative_feedback_tunning_scheme_for_the_multiloop_PID_control_of_a_UAV.pdf).
- Global optimization algorithms (Genetic Algorithms, Particle Swarm Optimization, gradient-based search) produce gains that optimize multi-objective cost (rise time, overshoot, control effort). GA/PSO have been shown effective for improving rise/settle times vs manual methods, with the caveat that they require a reliable model or many evaluations in simulation [9] [Genetic Algorithm Based PID Controller Tuning](https://onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/10.1155/2014/791230), [14] [PSO–PID Controller for Quadcopter UAV (PDF)](https://www.researchgate.net/publication/372176724_PSO-PID_Controller_for_Quadcopter_UAV_Index_Performance_Comparison).
- Commercial / toolkit autotuners (e.g., MATLAB/Simulink PID autotuner workflows) are practical for baseline gains and provide closed-loop validated gains in simulation/HIL [5] [PID Autotuning for UAV Quadcopter - MATLAB & Simulink](https://www.mathworks.com/help/slcontrol/ug/pid-controller-tuning-for-a-uav-quadcopter.html).

### 2) Gain scheduling and flight-state partitioning
- Create a small set of gain-sets mapped to measurable flight states (e.g., hover, low-speed cruise, high-speed cruise, high-payload, aggressive maneuvering). Transition logic uses measured airspeed, collective throttle, attitude rates, or payload sensor. Gain scheduling preserves PID simplicity while covering a wide envelope with deterministic switching [6] [UAV PID tuning guide / PX4](https://docs.px4.io/main/en/config_mc/pid_tuning_guide_multicopter).
- Advantage: low compute, straightforward verification. Limitation: requires correct state detection and smoothing to avoid discontinuities.

### 3) Adaptive / self-tuning PID controllers
- Adaptive PID automatically updates gains online based on performance or estimated plant parameters. Implementations include model-reference adaptive PID and adaptive laws that track changing inertia or time constants (e.g., payload change) [7] [Development of Adaptive Control System for Aerial Vehicles - MDPI](https://www.mdpi.com/2076-3417/13/23/12940), [23] [Adaptive PID-like controller for quadrotor](https://www.mdpi.com/2226-4310/11/12/980).
- Self-tuning variants often combine recursive least squares for parameter estimation with gain recalculation. They improve robustness to slow-changing conditions but need careful design to avoid instability from aggressive adaptation.

### 4) Fuzzy logic and hybrid fuzzy-PID
- Fuzzy-PID (FPID) uses fuzzy inference to adjust PID gains or directly produce control corrections based on heuristic rule sets reflecting pilot/engineer knowledge (e.g., increase D on high rate error). FPID improves handling of nonlinearities and imprecise knowledge, and is widely used for attitude/altitude loops [22] [Hybrid adaptive PID: NNPID+FPID - PLOS ONE](https://journals.plos.org/plosone/article?id=10.1371/journal.pone.0331036), [44] [Fuzzy self-tuning PID (PDF)](https://pdfs.semanticscholar.org/8b4b/5062158e3549ea80ca09f207bc730359530f.pdf).

### 5) Neural network augmentation and PIDNN
- Neural networks can be used to: (a) estimate inverse dynamics for feedforward terms, (b) predict required gain adjustments, or (c) replace parts of the controller (NNPID). Studies show NN-augmented PID reduces tracking error and shortens regulation times in demanding trajectories [12] [Neural Network PID applications](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11679864/), [20] [Neural network PID optimisation examples (MDPI)](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11679864/).

### 6) Reinforcement Learning (RL) and online learning
- RL methods can learn gain-scheduling or direct mapping from state to gains/actions in simulation then fine-tune online. RL-based online fine-tuning achieved smaller attitude errors than manual tuning in experimental work, but requires careful reward shaping and safe exploration strategies [4] [Reinforcement Learning Based Prediction of PID Controller Gains (arXiv)](https://arxiv.org/html/2502.04552v1), [2] [Enhancing UAV Altitude Control: PID Tuning with Reinforcement (IEEE)](https://ieeexplore.ieee.org/document/11014809/).
- RL offers high adaptivity but introduces challenges for sample efficiency, explainability and safety certification.

### 7) Fractional-order PID and advanced controller forms
- Fractional-order PID controllers (PI^λD^μ) add extra tuning degrees (fractional integrator/derivative orders) that can improve robustness and hovering stability in some studies [7] [Development of Adaptive Control System for Aerial Vehicles - MDPI](https://www.mdpi.com/2076-3417/13/23/12940).
- Alternative/advanced approaches such as cascade Model Predictive Control (MPC) or switching to MPC for demanding regimes have shown improved performance in maneuverability and disturbance rejection, but at higher computational cost [31] [Cascade MPC for UAVs](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S2772671124004169).

### 8) Engineering-level enhancements (filters, anti-windup, feedforward)
- Derivative filtering (D-term low-pass), notch filters for motor/airframe resonances, anti-windup schemes (conditional integration or back-calculation), and feedforward terms (throttle/airspeed dependent) substantially improve closed-loop robustness and reduce actuator saturation [6] [UAV PID tuning principles](https://theuavtech.com/wp-content/uploads/2020/10/UAV-Tech-PID-Tuning-Principles.pdf), [5] [PX4 multicopter PID guide](https://docs.px4.io/main/en/config_mc/pid_tuning_guide_multicopter).
- Increasing control loop frequency (up to the sensors/actuator bandwidth) improves disturbance rejection, but must respect computational and sensor noise limits [6], [5].

## Strategies to optimally select and adjust PID parameters
This section provides concrete, evidence-based strategies and a practical workflow for selecting and adapting gains across operational states.

### 1) Define objectives and metrics
- Choose performance metrics aligned with mission: tracking RMS error, rise time, settling time, overshoot, actuator saturation, energy consumption, robustness to wind, and safety margins. Multi-objective optimization is recommended rather than a single metric [22] [PID control survey](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/abs/pii/S1367578823000640), [42] [Stability & Performance metrics - NASA](https://ntrs.nasa.gov/api/citations/20100024263/downloads/20100024263.pdf).

### 2) Baseline development: model, simulate, autotune
- Build dynamics model or perform system identification at representative operating points. Use HIL/simulation to validate candidate gains and to run optimization safely [10] [MATLAB autotuning example](https://www.mathworks.com/help/slcontrol/ug/pid-controller-tuning-for-a-uav-quadcopter.html).
- Apply autotuning (relay/Ziegler-Nichols with caution), gradient-based autotune or GA/PSO to obtain initial gains. GA/PSO often outperform hand methods on multi-objective metrics but require careful fitness design and sufficient evaluation data [9], [14].

### 3) Gain scheduling and small set of validated gain-sets
- Partition flight envelope into a limited number (2–6) of states and derive validated gain-sets for each (hover, slow cruise, fast cruise, heavy payload, aggressive acro). Use smooth interpolation or hysteresis-based switching to avoid chatter [6] [PX4 Guide](https://docs.px4.io/main/en/config_mc/pid_tuning_guide_multicopter).

### 4) Implement robust online adaptation with safety guards
- If employing adaptive/self-tuning/fuzzy/NN/RL:
  - Start with conservative adaptation gains (slow adaptation) and bounded gain ranges.
  - Include supervisory logic that monitors stability indicators (e.g., growth in attitude oscillation, control saturation, sensor faults) and reverts to safe baseline gains if thresholds exceeded [7] [Adaptive control professional autopilots](https://www.embention.com/news/adaptive-control-uav-autopilots/).
  - Log adaptation history and rationale for post-flight analysis.
- Combined methods such as hybrid NNPID+FPID showed improved tracking and convergence speed in experiments [3] [NNPID+FPID PLOS One](https://journals.plos.org/plosone/article?id=10.1371/journal.pone.0331036).

### 5) Regular re-identification / periodic autotune
- Schedule periodic re-identification or autotune after airframe changes, payload changes, or after detected performance drift. Use HIL to test new gains before flight.

### 6) Use feedforward and command-shaping where possible
- For predictable setpoints (waypoints, trajectory-following), add feedforward terms (model-based thrust/torque commands) and command shaping (minimum jerk/snap) to reduce burden on feedback PID and reduce overshoot [31] [Cascade MPC & feedforward improvements](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S2772671124004169).

### 7) Practical anti-windup, filters and sampling considerations
- Implement anti-windup (back-calculation or conditional integrate) to avoid integral saturation during large commands.
- Use derivative filtering (low-pass on D term) to reduce noise amplification; tune the filter cutoff to trade off responsiveness and noise.
- Select control loop rate proportional to actuator/sensor bandwidth (typical multi-rotor attitude loops run 250–1,000 Hz depending on hardware), remembering that higher loop rates amplify sensor noise and require more compute [6] [UAV PID tuning principles](https://theuavtech.com/wp-content/uploads/2020/10/UAV-Tech-PID-Tuning-Principles.pdf).

## Comparative analysis: methods vs trade-offs
- Manual/heuristic tuning (Ziegler/Nichols, trial-and-error)
  - Pros: simple, well-known, easy to validate.
  - Cons: narrow validity range, suboptimal in agility and disturbance rejection.
- Offline optimization (GA/PSO, gradient search, IFT)
  - Pros: finds multi-objective optima, good for baseline; supports gain-scheduling.
  - Cons: requires model or many evaluations; may overfit to simulated conditions.
- Gain scheduling
  - Pros: low compute; deterministic; easy to validate per operating point.
  - Cons: requires reliable state classification; discontinuities must be smoothed.
- Adaptive / Self-tuning PID
  - Pros: adapts to slow or predictable changes (payload, battery).
  - Cons: potential instability if adaptation gains too high; needs supervision.
- Fuzzy/NN augmentation
  - Pros: handles nonlinearities; good empirical performance improvements.
  - Cons: heuristic design (fuzzy) or opaque models (NN) complicate certification.
- Reinforcement learning
  - Pros: can discover complex gain policies and high performance behavior.
  - Cons: sample inefficiency, safety during exploration, explainability, validation burden.
- Fractional-order PID / MPC
  - Pros: improved robustness/precision in some regimes.
  - Cons: higher computational cost, more complex tuning.

## Recommended hybrid architecture (practical, evidence-based)
1. Baseline cascaded PID with well-chosen anti-windup, D-filtering and feedforward. Derive baseline gains via model-based design and autotune in sim/HIL [5] [MATLAB autotune](https://www.mathworks.com/help/slcontrol/ug/pid-controller-tuning-for-a-uav-quadcopter.html), [6] [PX4 Guide](https://docs.px4.io/main/en/config_mc/pid_tuning_guide_multicopter).
2. Implement a small gain-scheduled map covering typical flight states (hover, cruise, heavy payload) with smooth interpolation.
3. Add a supervised adaptive layer (fuzzy logic or lightweight NN) that provides incremental gain adjustments within safety bounds; log all changes and include fallback to baseline gains on anomaly [3] [Hybrid adaptive PID (PLOS)](https://journals.plos.org/plosone/article?id=10.1371/journal.pone.0331036).
4. Use offline optimization (GA/IFT) periodically to refine gain-sets and update scheduling thresholds based on logged flight data.
5. For research or specialized missions where computational power and certification are acceptable, consider RL policies or model predictive layers for aggressive regimes—only after rigorous sim-to-real validation and safety supervisors are in place [4] [RL tuning arXiv](https://arxiv.org/html/2502.04552v1).
6. Maintain a safety supervisor that monitors oscillation, actuator saturation and other stability flags and enforces immediate reversion to a validated "safe" gain-set when necessary [7] [Embention adaptive autopilots](https://www.embention.com/news/adaptive-control-uav-autopilots/).

## Implementation roadmap (step-by-step)
1. Instrumentation: ensure accurate IMU, baro/GPS/air-speed, motor ESC telemetry, and high-fidelity logging.
2. Identification & modeling: identify plant dynamics at 3–5 operating points (hover, slow cruise, fast cruise, high payload).
3. Baseline tuning: use closed-loop autotuning or classical iterative tuning (relay/Z-N variants) to get starting gains; validate in sim/HIL [5] [MathWorks example](https://www.mathworks.com/help/slcontrol/ug/pid-controller-tuning-for-a-uav-quadcopter.html).
4. Offline optimization: run GA/PSO/IFT across scenarios to derive gain sets and scheduling boundaries [9], [10].
5. Implement anti-windup, D-filter, notch filters for resonances, and feedforward where model is available [6].
6. Implement gain scheduling with smooth interpolation and hysteresis; test transitions extensively in HIL.
7. Add adaptive/fuzzy/NN module constrained by bounded gain changes and monitored by safety supervisor [3], [12].
8. Flight test progression: tethered/safe area hover -> limited maneuvers -> full envelope missions. Increase adaptation aggressiveness only after stability verified.
9. Maintain logs and periodically re-tune based on drift or configuration changes.

## Empirical results and case studies (selected)
- MATLAB/Simulink autotuner: tuned multirotor completed a four-waypoint mission significantly faster with tuned gains versus untuned baseline [5] [MathWorks example](https://www.mathworks.com/help/slcontrol/ug/pid-controller-tuning-for-a-uav-quadcopter.html).
- Hybrid NNPID+FPID: simulation and experiments showed improved helical trajectory tracking versus standalone fuzzy or NN approaches [3] [PLOS One NNPID+FPID](https://journals.plos.org/plosone/article?id=10.1371/journal.pone.0331036).
- RL-based online tuning: achieved smaller attitude tracking errors than hand-tuned controllers in experimental work, demonstrating viability for online fine tuning when safety constraints are enforced [4] [RL tuning arXiv](https://arxiv.org/html/2502.04552v1).
- Fractional-order PID: studies reported improved hovering stability and robustness versus classical PID in simulated and experimental tests [7] [MDPI adaptive control](https://www.mdpi.com/2076-3417/13/23/12940).

## Limitations, risks and open research directions
- Stability guarantees: adaptive, NN and RL methods can improve performance but complicate theoretical stability proofs and certification; supervisory fallback and bounded adaptation mitigate risk [22] [PID survey](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/abs/pii/S1367578823000640).
- Sim-to-real transfer: learning-based methods require domain randomization and careful HIL to ensure transferability.
- Sample-efficiency and safety: RL methods are often data hungry; safe-exploration research is needed for online field learning.
- Computational cost: advanced methods (MPC, high-order NN) may exceed payload compute budgets on small UAVs; careful profiling required [31].

## Conclusion and practical recommendations
- For most operational UAVs, the highest-value approach is a hybrid: a robust baseline PID (tuned in model/HIL) + a small, validated gain-scheduling map + conservative bounded online adaptation (fuzzy or light NN) and strong safety supervision. Use global optimization/IFT periodically to refresh gain sets based on logged flight data. Reserve computationally expensive or non-deterministic methods (full RL, MPC) for specialized platforms where compute, safety validation and certification resources exist.
- Key engineering measures (anti-windup, D-term filtering, feedforward, correct loop frequency and HIL testing) are low-cost improvements that materially improve practical performance across conditions and should be implemented regardless of higher-level adaptation method.

article:
# Comparative analysis of classic asset-allocation models (Mean–Variance, Black–Litterman) vs. deep learning models — risk measurement, return prediction, asset allocation, and hybrid design

## Executive summary
Classic portfolio models (Markowitz mean–variance / MVO and Black–Litterman / BL) are mathematically transparent, low-dimensional and rely on return expectations and covariance structure to measure risk and build allocations; they are sensitive to estimation error and rely on strong distributional or subjective-view assumptions [Mean–Variance Analysis](https://www.investopedia.com/terms/m/meanvariance-analysis.asp)[1], [Black–Litterman Model](https://www.investopedia.com/terms/b/black-litterman_model.asp)[4]. Deep learning (DL) and deep reinforcement learning (DRL) can capture non-linear, high-dimensional signals (including unstructured data) and produce time-varying trading/allocation policies, but they are data-hungry, harder to interpret, and vulnerable to overfitting and regime shifts [Deep learning in investing](https://www.sparklinecapital.com/post/deep-learning-in-investing-opportunity-in-unstructured-data)[13], [AI reshaping financial modelling](https://www.nature.com/articles/s44387-025-00030-w)[11]. Combining the two paradigms is feasible and promising: practical hybrids use DL to generate views/forecasts or latent risk factors, then feed those into constrained optimization (e.g., BL or regularized MVO), or use DL/DRL as an outer policy with classical models enforcing risk controls — producing better generalization, interpretability and robustness when implemented with strong validation and governance [Objective BL via deep learning](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/abs/pii/S0957417425024856)[6], [LLM-Enhanced Black-Litterman](https://arxiv.org/html/2504.14345v2)[7], [Tackling portfolio optimisers limitations with ML (CFA UK)](https://www.cfauk.org/pi-listing/embracing-machine-learning-to-tackle-portfolio-optimisers-limitations)[12].

---

## 1. Brief overview of the classical models

### 1.1 Markowitz Mean–Variance Optimization (MVO)
- Core idea: Choose portfolio weights that maximize expected return for a given level of variance (or minimize variance for a target return). It uses expected returns vector and covariance matrix as inputs. [Mean–Variance Analysis](https://www.investopedia.com/terms/m/meanvariance-analysis.asp)[1], [Modern portfolio theory](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Modern_portfolio_theory)[2], [Mean–Variance and CAPM (technical)](https://www.columbia.edu/~mh2078/FoundationsFE/MeanVariance-CAPM.pdf)[3].
- Risk measurement: Portfolio variance (or standard deviation). Covariance structure drives diversification gains.
- Return prediction: Exogenous expected-return vector (often estimated from historical averages, factor models or forecasts).
- Allocation mechanics: Quadratic optimization problem; solutions can be extremely sensitive to small changes in inputs (estimation error), producing concentrated or extreme weights.
- Strengths: Conceptually simple, analytically tractable, interpretable; closed-form solutions and clear risk–return trade-off.
- Weaknesses: Assumes mean and variance capture investor preferences; input sensitivity and estimation error (especially expected returns) produce unstable allocations [3].

### 1.2 Black–Litterman (BL)
- Core idea: Start from market equilibrium (implicit equilibrium returns from market-cap weights) and blend those with investor views to form posterior expected returns; feed those into an MVO to get allocations [Black–Litterman Model](https://www.investopedia.com/terms/b/black-litterman_model.asp)[4], [MathWorks BL guide](https://www.mathworks.com/help/finance/black-litterman-portfolio-optimization.html)[5].
- Risk measurement: Uses the same covariance structure as MVO; BL primarily addresses expected-return estimation rather than altering risk measurement.
- Return prediction: Produces regularized expected-return estimates by combining a prior (market-implied) and views with explicitly modeled confidence in views.
- Allocation mechanics: Produces smoother, more intuitive allocations than vanilla MVO when views are modest and view-confidence is calibrated.
- Strengths: Reduces extreme allocations caused by noisy expected-return inputs; formalizes how to incorporate subjective views.
- Weaknesses: Requires specification of views and their confidences (subjective); performance sensitive to view specification and covariance assumptions; still depends on covariance estimates and can fail in crises [On the Black–Litterman Model: Learning to Do Better](https://www.pm-research.com/content/iijjfds/4/3/66)[15].

---

## 2. Overview of deep learning approaches in asset allocation

### 2.1 Classes of DL applications
- Prediction-based: Neural nets (MLPs, LSTMs, Transformers) trained to predict returns, signals, or latent factors from structured and unstructured data (prices, fundamentals, macro, news, alternative data) [Deep learning in investing](https://www.sparklinecapital.com/post/deep-learning-in-investing-opportunity-in-unstructured-data)[13].
- Policy-based / DRL: Agents learn an allocation/trading policy directly (reward = risk-adjusted return), yielding dynamic, path-dependent allocation rules [Deep reinforcement learning for asset allocation](https://ui.adsabs.harvard.edu/abs/2020arXiv201004404A/abstract)[8].
- Generative and representation learning: Autoencoders, VAEs, or contrastive methods to find latent risk factors or compressed state representations useful for downstream allocation or stress testing.

### 2.2 Risk measurement in DL systems
- Implicit risk modeling: DL models often learn conditional return distributions or quantiles (e.g., using quantile losses, heteroskedastic outputs), or estimate tail risks via generative models; risk is not limited to variance but can be learned as conditional Value-at-Risk / Expected Shortfall [AI reshaping financial modelling](https://www.nature.com/articles/s44387-025-00030-w)[11].
- Hybrid explicit constraints: DL policies are frequently constrained (penalized) for turnover, leverage, CVaR, or exposed to risk models as part of training (e.g., penalties on volatility) to ensure practical deployments [High-dimensional multi-period portfolio allocation using deep ...](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S1059056025001595)[14].

### 2.3 Return prediction in DL systems
- Advantage: Ability to find complex, nonlinear interactions and to fuse unstructured data (news, text, satellite, alternative datasets) with structured numeric data, improving signal extraction when signal exists [Deep learning in investing](https://www.sparklinecapital.com/post/deep-learning-in-investing-opportunity-in-unstructured-data)[13].
- Limitations: Financial return predictability is low and unstable; increasing model complexity does not always improve out-of-sample performance—optimal complexity may be lower for financial time series than for unstructured domains [The Virtue of Complexity in Return Prediction](https://economics.yale.edu/sites/default/files/2024-01/The%20Journal%20of%20Finance%20-%202023%20-%20KELLY%20-%20The%20Virtue%20of%20Complexity%20in%20Return%20Prediction%20%281%29.pdf)[10], [Instability of Return Prediction Models](https://rady.ucsd.edu/_files/faculty-research/timmermann/instability.pdf)[9].
- Data demands: DL models need long histories, high-frequency observations, or multiple data modalities to avoid overfitting.

### 2.4 Allocation mechanics with DL
- DRL can produce allocation policies that adapt to changing regimes and produce superior backtest metrics in published studies, especially when transaction costs and realistic constraints are modeled carefully [Deep reinforcement learning ...](https://ui.adsabs.harvard.edu/abs/2020arXiv201004404A/abstract)[8], [High-dimensional multi-period ...](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S1059056025001595)[14].
- Practical issues: DL outputs can be extreme/unintuitive without regularization; lack of interpretability complicates risk governance [Measuring model risk-adjusted performance of ML](https://jfin-swufe.springeropen.com/articles/10.1186/s40854-022-00366-1)[15].

---

## 3. Direct comparison: risk measurement, return prediction, and allocation

### 3.1 Risk measurement
- MVO / BL: Use covariance / variance as core risk measure; transparent, mathematically tractable but blind to non-Gaussian tails, conditional heteroskedasticity, and nonlinearity. Covariance estimates can be unstable and sensitive to estimation error [Mean–Variance Analysis](https://www.investopedia.com/terms/m/meanvariance-analysis.asp)[1], [Mean–Variance-CAPM PDF](https://www.columbia.edu/~mh2078/FoundationsFE/MeanVariance-CAPM.pdf)[3].
- DL/DRL: Can learn conditional risk measures (heteroskedasticity, tail behavior, scenario-dependent risk), and incorporate unstructured signals. But learned risk representations can be opaque and require substantial data + careful validation [AI reshaping financial modelling](https://www.nature.com/articles/s44387-025-00030-w)[11].

Practical take: Use classical covariance-based measures for transparency and regulatory reporting, and supplement with DL-based conditional risk estimates (e.g., modelled CVaR, scenario probabilities) for dynamic risk management.

### 3.2 Return prediction
- MVO/BL: Rely on point estimates of expected returns. BL mitigates MVO’s sensitivity by shrinking toward equilibrium returns and incorporating views, but still relies on the quality and calibration of views [Black–Litterman Model](https://www.investopedia.com/terms/b/black-litterman_model.asp)[4].
- DL: Can extract richer predictive signals from many modalities, non-linear relationships, and long lag structures. However, financial return predictability is low and non-stationary; complex DL models sometimes provide little incremental out-of-sample improvement over simpler models unless they exploit alternative/unstructured data or very large datasets [The Virtue of Complexity in Return Prediction](https://economics.yale.edu/sites/default/files/2024-01/The%20Journal%20of%20Finance%20-%202023%20-%20KELLY%20-%20The%20Virtue%20of%20Complexity%20in%20Return%20Prediction%20%281%29.pdf)[10], [Instability of Return Prediction Models](https://rady.ucsd.edu/_files/faculty-research/timmermann/instability.pdf)[9].

Practical take: Combine structural priors (BL equilibrium) with DL forecasts as probabilistic views or as extra features; treat DL outputs probabilistically and regularize heavily.

### 3.3 Asset allocation
- MVO: Static or single-period optimization that can produce unstable allocations without regularization or shrinkage techniques.
- BL: Produces smoother allocations by Bayesian blending of market equilibrium and views; still single-period unless extended.
- DL/DRL: Produce dynamic, potentially multi-period allocation policies that optimize time-sequence rewards, and can incorporate transaction costs, market impact, or path-dependent constraints. But they require careful training, regularization, and real-world constraints to avoid overfit strategies that fail live [Deep reinforcement learning ...](https://ui.adsabs.harvard.edu/abs/2020arXiv201004404A/abstract)[8].

Practical take: Use DL/DRL for tactical and dynamic allocation and classical models (BL/MVO with shrinkage) for strategic/core allocations and for governance/limit-setting.

---

## 4. Feasibility and concrete ways to combine strengths

Multiple hybrid strategies have been proposed and demonstrated in research and practice. Key patterns:

### 4.1 Use DL to generate views or signals that feed into Black–Litterman
- Mechanism: Train DL or LLMs to produce expected-return views (point forecasts plus confidence/uncertainty estimates). Use those as the view vector and confidence matrix in BL to produce posterior expected returns which are then optimized via MVO or constrained optimization.
- Evidence/examples: Research showing objective BL views via DL and LLM-enhanced BL frameworks produce better out-of-sample performance in many settings [Objective Black–Litterman views through deep learning](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/abs/pii/S0957417425024856)[6], [LLM-Enhanced Black-Litterman](https://arxiv.org/html/2504.14345v2)[7].
- Practical advantage: DL supplies rich, multi-modal views; BL regularizes them with market equilibrium and explicit confidence levels, reducing extreme weights.

Suggested pipeline:
1. Train DL predictive model to produce expected returns and predictive uncertainty (e.g., via ensembles, Bayesian NN, quantile regression).
2. Map predictive uncertainty to BL view-confidence matrix.
3. Run BL to obtain posterior expected returns.
4. Feed into constrained MVO (regularized / robustified) for final weights.

### 4.2 Regularize/robustify MVO with ML/DL factor estimates and covariances
- Mechanism: Use DL/representation learning to extract latent factors (autoencoders, factor nets) or to produce better covariance estimates (shrinkage, nonlinear factor structures). Feed those into MVO with shrinkage methods for more stable covariance matrices.
- Evidence: High-dimensional DL-based portfolio allocation literature shows value in compressing state-space and improving multi-period allocation [High-dimensional multi-period portfolio allocation using deep ...](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S1059056025001595)[14].
- Practical advantage: Retains interpretability of MVO while improving input estimates using ML.

### 4.3 Use BL/MVO as constraints or priors inside DRL training
- Mechanism: Incorporate BL-implied portfolios or MVO weight distributions as priors/penalties inside the DRL reward or policy regularization term to keep DL policies close to economically sensible allocations.
- Practical advantage: Combines adaptability of DRL with stability and economic plausibility of classical portfolios.

### 4.4 Ensembles and meta-optimization (stacking)
- Mechanism: Compute candidate portfolios from multiple engines (MVO, BL, DL forecasts/DRL policy) and use a meta-optimizer (convex combination, regularized regression, or a risk-parity allocator) that learns weights for combining candidate portfolios with stability constraints.
- Practical advantage: Diversifies model risk and often improves robustness.

### 4.5 Stress testing and scenario generation with DL
- Mechanism: Use generative DL models to create realistic adversarial or rare-event scenarios; evaluate classical portfolios (MVO/BL) and DL policies across those scenarios for robust design.
- Practical advantage: Identifies failure modes that single-method backtests miss [AI reshaping financial modelling](https://www.nature.com/articles/s44387-025-00030-w)[11].

---

## 5. Implementation roadmap and experimental design

### 5.1 Data & features
- Core market data: prices, returns, volumes, market caps, yields, option-implied volatilities.
- Fundamentals & macro: earnings, balance-sheet metrics, CPI, unemployment.
- Alternative/unstructured: news/text (NLP), sentiment, satellite/ESG.
- Label engineering: target horizons (daily, monthly), return definitions (excess returns), risk measures for supervised losses (quantiles, CVaR).

### 5.2 Model building steps
1. Baseline: Implement MVO and BL (market-implied returns + a few hand-crafted views) to set a strategic benchmark [Black–Litterman Model](https://www.investopedia.com/terms/b/black-litterman_model.asp)[4], [MathWorks BL guide](https://www.mathworks.com/help/finance/black-litterman-portfolio-optimization.html)[5].
2. DL forecasting: Train predictive models (LSTM/Transformer/MLP) to produce point forecasts and uncertainty estimates. Use ensembling, dropout-as-Bayesian approximations, or explicit probabilistic heads for uncertainty.
3. Hybrid plug-ins:
   - Plug DL forecasts + uncertainties into BL as objective views (pipeline 4.1).
   - Use DL to produce latent factors and better covariance estimates for MVO.
   - Train DRL with BL/MVO-derived risk penalties.
4. Meta-learner: Learn convex weights for combining final candidate portfolios, with constraints on turnover, leverage, and concentration.

### 5.3 Validation and backtesting
- Use rolling walk-forward evaluation, nested cross-validation, multiple market regimes and realistic transaction-cost / market-impact models. Evaluate stability under parameter shifts and adopt conservative hyperparameter choices to avoid overfitting [Instability of Return Prediction Models](https://rady.ucsd.edu/_files/faculty-research/timmermann/instability.pdf)[9].
- Metrics: Sharpe ratio, Sortino, Information Ratio, maximum drawdown, tail metrics (CVaR), turnover, transaction costs, robustness across regimes.
- Model risk: measure model-contribution to tail risk and perform adversarial stress tests using generative scenario models [Measuring model risk-adjusted performance of ML](https://jfin-swufe.springeropen.com/articles/10.1186/s40854-022-00366-1)[15].

### 5.4 Governance, deployability and explainability
- Governance: clear AI governance, model risk management, documentation and centralized standards for data, model lifecycle and monitoring [AI governance foundations].
- Explainability: Use interpretable components where possible; apply post-hoc tools (SHAP, LIME) and decompositions to produce understandable views for BL; keep a classical “fallback” allocator for live risk limits [Tackling portfolio optimisers limitations with ML (CFA UK)](https://www.cfauk.org/pi-listing/embracing-machine-learning-to-tackle-portfolio-optimisers-limitations)[12].
- Operational constraints: latency, compute cost, and integration with execution systems.

---

## 6. Common pitfalls and mitigations

- Overfitting and look-ahead bias: Use strict data hygiene, time-aware splits and realistic transaction costs.
- Non-stationarity and regime shifts: Use rolling retraining, domain adaptation, or causal representation learning to improve extrapolation [The Virtue of Complexity in Return Prediction](https://economics.yale.edu/sites/default/files/2024-01/The%20Journal%20of%20Finance%20-%202023%20-%20KELLY%20-%20The%20Virtue%20of%20Complexity%20in%20Return%20Prediction%20%281%29.pdf)[10], [Emerging synergies in causality and DGMs](https://arxiv.org/html/2301.12351v4) (for causal ideas).
- Model opacity and regulatory risk: Use BL/MVO to anchor decisions and provide a transparent “why” for allocations; produce audit trails for DL outputs that feed BL views [LLM-Enhanced Black-Litterman](https://arxiv.org/html/2504.14345v2)[7].
- Data quality and survivorship bias: Careful preprocessing, using full history, and sanitized alternative data sources.

---

## 7. Example experimental design (three hybrid variants)

1. DL-as-view → Black–Litterman → Regularized MVO
   - Train ensemble DL model to forecast 1‑month returns + predictive variance.
   - Map forecasts to BL views and use predictive variance → view confidence.
   - Run BL → posterior returns → L2-regularized MVO with turnover penalties.
   - Evaluate with rolling walk-forward, transaction costs and stress scenarios.

2. DL factor compression → MVO covariance + DRL tactical overlay
   - Use autoencoder/contrastive net to produce 10 latent factors (learned from multi-modal data).
   - Use factors to compute stable covariance for MVO strategic allocation.
   - Train DRL tactical overlay to tilt between strategic weights and short-term alpha while constrained by maximum tracking error and CVaR.

3. Ensemble stacking
   - Produce candidate portfolios: EW, MVO (shrinkage), BL(with analyst views), DL-forecast MVO, DRL policy.
   - Meta-optimizer fits convex combination under constraints (max turnover, max tracking error).
   - Backtest and measure risk-adjusted returns and stability.

---

## 8. Practical recommendations (prioritized)
1. Start with a robust classical baseline (MVO + BL) to provide a transparent strategic anchor and risk-limits [Black–Litterman Model](https://www.investopedia.com/terms/b/black-litterman_model.asp)[4], [MathWorks BL guide](https://www.mathworks.com/help/finance/black-litterman-portfolio-optimization.html)[5].
2. Develop DL models initially as signal/view generators (not as sole decision-makers); calibrate their uncertainty and feed into BL or risk models [Objective Black–Litterman views through deep learning](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/abs/pii/S0957417425024856)[6].
3. Emphasize rigorous, time-aware validation, realistic costs and stress testing. Monitor out-of-sample stability; prefer simpler DL architectures when data is limited [Instability of Return Prediction Models](https://rady.ucsd.edu/_files/faculty-research/timmermann/instability.pdf)[9], [The Virtue of Complexity in Return Prediction](https://economics.yale.edu/sites/default/files/2024-01/The%20Journal%20of%20Finance%20-%202023%20-%20KELLY%20-%20The%20Virtue%20of%20Complexity%20in%20Return%20Prediction%20%281%29.pdf)[10].
4. Use interpretable intermediates: DL-derived views should be accompanied by rationale and uncertainty metrics so BL/MVO can regularize and produce explainable allocations [LLM-Enhanced Black-Litterman](https://arxiv.org/html/2504.14345v2)[7].
5. Maintain governance: model risk management, monitoring, retraining policies and an auditable pipeline before production deployment [Tackling portfolio optimisers limitations with ML (CFA UK)](https://www.cfauk.org/pi-listing/embracing-machine-learning-to-tackle-portfolio-optimisers-limitations)[12].

---

## 9. Conclusion
Classic models (MVO, BL) provide interpretability, clear risk accounting and regulatory-friendly outputs but are limited by linearity assumptions and estimation sensitivity. Deep learning brings the capacity to harvest complex signals, fuse unstructured data, and produce adaptive multi-period policies, but requires careful control to avoid overfitting, opacity and instability. Hybrid frameworks that use DL to generate probabilistic views or latent factors and then use BL/MVO (or BL-informed constraints) to produce allocations combine the strengths of both worlds, improving predictive power while retaining economic interpretability and risk governance. Success depends on careful experimental design, robust validation, stress testing, and institutional model governance.
